case: A 70 year old man has prostate cancer and will receive external beam radiation. You must decide on hormone therapy based on his risk group.
question: How long do you give androgen deprivation by risk group, including node-positive disease?
answer: Unfavorable intermediate risk gets 6 months of ADT. High risk gets 24 months of ADT. Node-positive disease gets 24 months of ADT plus abiraterone.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Prostate EBRT Hypofrac

case: A man with high risk prostate cancer is planned for moderately hypofractionated IMRT. MRI shows a PI-RADS 5 nodule in the left peripheral zone.
question: Describe your target volumes, doses and the intraprostatic boost.
answer: CTV is the prostate and seminal vesicles, proximal vesicles for intermediate risk and the full vesicles for high risk, to 60 Gy, with PTV of 7 millimeters and 5 millimeters posteriorly. The PI-RADS 4 or 5 nodule is the GTV for a focal boost to 67 Gy, with the PTV cropped 2 millimeters off the urethra and urethra D0.035cc under 110 to 120 percent of the prostate dose. Daily kV or CBCT aligned to fiducials.
key_points: CTV prostate plus seminal vesicles to 60 Gy
Full SV for high risk, proximal for intermediate
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Prostate EBRT Hypofrac

case: You are reviewing a moderately hypofractionated 60 Gy prostate IMRT plan.
question: What normal tissue constraints do you use?
answer: Rectum V60 under 1 to 8 percent, V40 under 50 to 55 percent, V20 under 85 percent, avoiding circumferential dose. Bladder V60 under 3 to 10 percent and V40 under 50 percent. Bowel bag D0.035cc under 45 to 48 Gy, colon max under 50, small bowel max under 40. Penile bulb V22 under 50 percent and femoral head max under 37 Gy.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Prostate EBRT Hypofrac

case: A man has high risk prostate cancer, PSA 30 and Gleason 8. You are deciding whether to treat the pelvic lymph nodes.
question: How do you decide on elective nodal radiation, and what are the nodal volumes and dose?
answer: I treat elective nodes for high risk disease and consider it when the Roach nodal risk exceeds 15 to 20 percent, calculated as two thirds of the PSA plus Gleason minus 6 times 10. The CTV is the common, external and internal iliac, obturator and presacral vessels plus 7 millimeters, cropped off muscle, bone, bladder and bowel, with a 7 millimeter PTV, to 44 Gy. Any gross node gets a GTV plus 5 millimeter PTV boosted to the highest dose constraints allow.
key_points: Treat if risk >15-20% or high risk
Common, external, internal iliac, obturator, presacral
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Prostate EBRT Hypofrac

case: A man with favorable intermediate risk prostate cancer and a 45 cc gland is treated with stereotactic body radiation.
question: Describe your SBRT dose, volumes and image guidance.
answer: 40 Gy in 5 fractions to the CTV and 36.25 Gy in 5 to the PTV, every other day. CTV is the prostate, and per PACE can include the proximal 1 centimeter of seminal vesicles for intermediate risk; PTV is 5 millimeters, 3 millimeters posteriorly. Daily kV or CBCT aligned to fiducials and a daily enema.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Prostate EBRT SBRT

case: You are reviewing a 5 fraction prostate SBRT plan, 40 Gy to the CTV.
question: What are your urethra, rectum, bladder and bowel constraints?
answer: Urethra D0.03cc under 43.5 Gy. Rectum D0.03cc under 41.2 Gy and V18 under 50 to 60 percent. Bladder D0.03cc under 43.5 Gy and V18 under 40 to 60 percent. Bowel D0.035cc under 27.5 to 30 Gy.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Prostate EBRT SBRT

case: A man with low risk prostate cancer chooses I-125 LDR seed implant monotherapy. He comes in for his pre-plan.
question: Describe the transrectal ultrasound volume study.
answer: About one week before the implant, in lithotomy with the pelvis flexed to raise the pubic arch and genitalia taped up. Prep the perineum, place a Foley with 120 cc in the bladder, and secure the TRUS to the table. Center the template on the prostate with base at zero and the rectal wall at row 1, then capture transverse images every 5 millimeters from base to apex plus a slice above and below, note length and volume, and contour prostate, bladder, anterior rectal wall and urethra.
key_points: Lithotomy, pelvis flexed to raise arch
Template: base zero, rectal wall row 1
Transverse images every 5 mm base to apex
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Prostate Brachy Monotherapy

case: A man is undergoing an I-125 prostate seed implant. At the end of the case, the intraoperative plain film seed count does not match the number implanted.
question: How do you conduct the implant and handle this, and what are the discharge instructions?
answer: Hold aspirin and anticoagulants 5 days, enema that morning, general anesthesia, match intraop images to the pre-plan using seminal vesicles and base, keep posterior needles about 5 millimeters off the rectum and weight needles peripherally to spare the urethra, verifying on sagittal and transverse ultrasound. After the plain film, do a cystoscopy with irrigation; if the seed count is still off get a chest x-ray to rule out seed migration. Discharge once voiding, with tamsulosin for 2 to 6 months, NSAIDs, and ciprofloxacin for about 3 days.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Prostate Brachy Monotherapy

case: A man had an I-125 LDR prostate implant to 145 Gy.
question: When do you perform post-implant dosimetry, and what target and organ metrics do you check?
answer: Post-implant dosimetry at 1 month. Target D90 at least 100 percent of prescription and V100 at least 90 percent, with V150 at or below 65 percent and V200 at or below 30 percent. Rectum V100 under 1 to 2 cc, bladder V100 under 1 to 2 cc, and urethra max under 150 percent.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Prostate Brachy Monotherapy

case: A 62 year old man had radical prostatectomy. His PSA at 8 weeks is 0.3. Another man's PSA was undetectable, then rose to 0.15 and 0.22.
question: How do you define PSA persistence versus PSA recurrence after prostatectomy?
answer: PSA persistence is failure of the postoperative PSA to become undetectable, as in the first man. PSA recurrence is an undetectable PSA after prostatectomy that later becomes detectable and rises on 2 or more determinations, or increases above 0.1, as in the second man.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Prostate Postoperative

case: A man is planned for salvage radiation to the prostate bed for a rising PSA after prostatectomy.
question: What are the borders of your prostate bed CTV?
answer: Anterior: posterior edge of the pubic bone below the top of the symphysis, and 1 to 2 centimeters of posterior bladder wall above. Posterior: anterior rectal wall and mesorectal fascia. Lateral: levator ani and obturator internus, or the sacrorectogenitopubic fascia above. Superior: cut end of the vas deferens or 3 to 4 centimeters above the top of the symphysis. Inferior: 8 to 12 millimeters below the vesicourethral anastomosis, or the slice above the penile bulb. PTV is 7 millimeters.
key_points: Anterior: posterior pubis, 1-2 cm bladder wall
Posterior: anterior rectal wall, mesorectal fascia
Superior: vas deferens cut end or 3-4 cm above symphysis
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Prostate Postoperative

case: You are reviewing a 66.6 Gy prostate bed salvage plan.
question: What bladder and rectal constraints do you use?
answer: Bladder V65 under 50 percent and V40 under 70 percent. Rectum V65 under 35 percent and V40 under 55 percent.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Prostate Postoperative

case: A 72 year old man with cT2 muscle invasive urothelial bladder cancer, no hydronephrosis, wants bladder preservation with trimodality therapy.
question: Describe your chemotherapy, simulation, volumes and dose.
answer: After maximal TURBT, concurrent mitomycin 12 milligrams per meter squared day 1 with 5-FU 500 milligrams per meter squared days 1 to 5 and 16 to 20. Simulate supine, arms up, lower vac-lock, empty bladder and empty rectum. CTV is the bladder and prostate; PTV is 1.5 centimeters, 2 centimeters over extravesical disease, to 55 Gy in 20 fractions with IMRT, or 64 Gy in 32 conventional fractions if treating nodes. Small bowel max under 52.5 Gy and daily CBCT.
key_points: CTV bladder and prostate, PTV 1.5 cm
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Bladder Intact

case: A man with muscle invasive bladder cancer and a single 1.5 centimeter pelvic node is treated with bladder-sparing chemoradiation in 20 fractions.
question: Which nodal regions do you include, and how do you dose the elective and involved nodes?
answer: Regional nodes include the hypogastric, obturator, internal and external iliac, perivesical, sacral and presacral nodes, with common iliacs as a site of secondary involvement when nodes are involved. Elective nodes get 44 Gy in 20 fractions. The gross node is a GTV plus 5 millimeter PTV boosted to the highest dose achievable within constraints.
key_points: Hypogastric, obturator, internal and external iliac
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Bladder Intact

case: A 66 year old woman underwent radical cystectomy for urothelial carcinoma. Pathology shows pT3b N1 disease with a positive soft tissue margin.
question: What are the indications for postoperative radiation, and what dose and volumes do you use?
answer: Indications are pT3 to 4a, node-positive, or margin-positive disease. Simulate arms up, lower vac-lock, empty rectum. 50.4 Gy in 28 fractions to the presacral, bilateral distal common iliac, external and internal iliac and obturator nodes, plus the cystectomy bed CTV for a positive margin, with a 5 to 7 millimeter PTV. The margin-positive or extranodal extension area is boosted to 54 to 60 Gy.
key_points: pT3-4a, node positive or margin positive
Presacral, distal common iliac, EI, II, obturator
Bed CTV only if margin positive
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Bladder Postop

case: A woman had cystectomy for urothelial carcinoma with a positive margin and will receive postoperative radiation.
question: Describe the borders of the postoperative bladder bed CTV.
answer: It covers tissue surrounding the intact empty bladder location, including uterus, tubes and upper vagina in women, or prostate and prostatic urethra in men, without intentionally including all clips, and small bowel is not carved out. Anterior is the mid-plane of the pubis above the pubis and posterior plane of the pubis below. Posteriorly it abuts the anterior third of the rectum. Superiorly 2 centimeters above the pubic symphysis. Inferiorly 2 to 3 millimeters above the penile bulb, or 1 centimeter below the obturator foramen.
key_points: Women: uterus, tubes, upper vagina; men: prostate
Do not carve out small bowel
Inferior: 1 cm below obturator foramen or above penile bulb
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Bladder Postop

case: A 35 year old man has stage IB pure seminoma after inguinal orchiectomy, with no prior groin or scrotal surgery, and chooses adjuvant radiation.
question: Describe your simulation, dose and para-aortic field.
answer: Supine with arms at side, vac-lock and a scrotal shield. 20 Gy in 10 fractions with AP-PA equally weighted fields. CTV is the aorta and IVC plus 1.2 to 1.9 centimeters covering paracaval, interaortocaval, preaortic and para-aortic nodes, PTV 5 millimeters, and block edge 7 millimeters beyond PTV. Borders are bottom of T10 or T11 to bottom of L5, about 10 centimeters wide covering the transverse processes. Kidney D50 under 8 Gy, and add inguinal and ipsilateral iliac nodes if prior pelvic surgery such as hernia repair or orchiopexy.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Seminoma Stage I

case: A 30 year old man has left testicular seminoma with a single 2.5 centimeter left para-aortic node.
question: Describe your field borders and dose including the boost.
answer: A modified dog leg AP-PA field to 20 Gy in 10 fractions, covering aorta and IVC from bottom of T10 or T11 plus the ipsilateral common, external and internal iliac vessels to the top of the acetabulum, with a 1.2 to 1.9 centimeter CTV, 5 millimeter PTV, and 7 millimeter block edge. The lower medial border runs from the contralateral L5 transverse process to the medial ipsilateral obturator foramen, and the lateral border from the ipsilateral L5 transverse process to the superolateral acetabulum. Then an AP-PA cone down to the node with 2 centimeter block margin, to a total of 36 Gy for a 2 to 3 centimeter node, or 30 Gy for 1 to 2 centimeters.
key_points: Cone down boost, 2 cm block margin
36 Gy for 2-3 cm node (30 Gy for 1-2 cm)
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Seminoma modified dog leg

case: A 68 year old man has a cT3 N1 squamous cell carcinoma of the proximal urethra and is not a surgical candidate.
question: What is your chemoradiation approach, doses, and nodal volumes?
answer: Definitive chemoradiation using bladder regimens such as cisplatin alone, 5-FU with mitomycin, or low dose gemcitabine. Gross primary to 66 to 70 Gy, gross nodes to 54 to 66 Gy, and elective nodes to 45 to 50.4 Gy with a 7 millimeter PTV. For a proximal male urethral primary the elective volume is the pelvic nodes; in women it is the inguinal and low pelvic nodes. A cT2 N0 tumor would not get elective nodal radiation.
key_points: Proximal male: pelvic nodes; female: inguinal
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Urethra Intact

case: A 60 year old man has a 3 centimeter T2 N0 squamous cell carcinoma of the penis and wants organ preservation with external beam.
question: Describe your simulation, technique, dose and nodal coverage.
answer: Supine, arms up, Foley in place, and immobilize the penile shaft with a wax mould, plastic cylinder or water bath, which also provides bolus; frog leg if treating inguinals. Parallel opposed lateral photons to the whole shaft, then cone down; IMRT if covering nodes. GTV plus 2 centimeters with bolus to 65 to 70 Gy, with concurrent cisplatin with or without 5-FU. For tumors under 4 centimeters consider inguinal nodes; for over 4 centimeters, T3-4 or node positive, treat the whole shaft and pelvic and inguinal nodes to 45 to 50.4 Gy.
key_points: Wax mould, cylinder or water bath
Over 4 cm/T3-4/N+: pelvic and inguinal nodes
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Penile EBRT

case: A 58 year old man has a 2.5 centimeter T1 N0 squamous cell carcinoma of the glans penis and prefers brachytherapy.
question: Describe the implant, dose and constraints.
answer: Interstitial implant under anesthesia or penile block with sedation, Foley to visualize the urethra, templates on either side for stabilization, and up to 6 needles perpendicular to the penis 1 centimeter apart, loaded after edema subsides. Target is GTV plus 1.5 to 2 centimeters. LDR 60 Gy at 0.5 to 0.6 Gy per hour over 5 days, or HDR 54 Gy in 3 Gy twice daily over 9 days. Penile V125 under 40 percent and V150 under 20 percent for necrosis; urethra V115 under 10 percent to limit stricture; avoid confluent 125 percent areas.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Penile Brachytherapy

case: A man had partial penectomy for squamous cell carcinoma with a positive margin. His inguinal node dissection showed two nodes with extracapsular extension.
question: What postoperative radiation do you give?
answer: For the positive margin, radiation to the primary site and scar to 45 to 60 Gy with IMRT, following intact guidelines if there is gross disease. For node-positive disease, or no or inadequate node dissection, give chemoradiation with cisplatin with or without 5-FU: gross nodes and extracapsular extension areas to 65 to 70 Gy, and the elective nodal regions to 45 to 50.4 Gy.
key_points: Primary site and scar for margin+
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: Penile Post-op

case: An 80 year old man with a 3.5 centimeter left renal cell carcinoma is medically inoperable and referred for SBRT.
question: What are the indications, simulation, dose and target volumes?
answer: T1 to T2a tumors up to 10 centimeters, with limited data above 7 centimeters. Supine, arms up, vac-lock, IV contrast, 4D CT and fiducials. 26 Gy in 1 fraction for tumors under 4 centimeters, or 42 Gy in 3 fractions if over 4. GTV on renal protocol MRI or CT, iGTV on all phases, PTV 3 to 5 millimeters, 3 millimeter OAR PRVs and 5 millimeters for bowel if abutting. Daily CBCT with triggered kV imaging to fiducials.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: RCC SBRT

case: You are reviewing a kidney SBRT plan for a renal cell carcinoma near the small bowel.
question: What spinal canal and bowel constraints do you use for 1 fraction and 3 fractions?
answer: Single fraction: spinal canal D0.03cc under 12 Gy, small bowel D0.03cc under 26 Gy with circumferential dose under 12.5, large bowel as low as possible, aiming under 26. Three fractions: spinal canal under 18 Gy, small bowel under 30 Gy with circumferential under 22.5, large bowel aiming under 42 Gy.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), GU row: RCC SBRT

case: A 45 year old woman had radical hysterectomy for a 3 centimeter cervical cancer with lymphovascular invasion and deep stromal invasion and needs adjuvant pelvic IMRT.
question: Describe your simulation and vaginal-parametrial CTV.
answer: Supine with full bladder and empty bladder scans, a vaginal marker at the cuff, and IV contrast. The vaginal-parametrial CTV extends posteriorly to the anterior rectal wall, about a third of the anterior mesorectum, anteriorly to the posterior bladder wall, laterally to the obturator nodal CTV or obturator internus, and covers 3.5 to 4 centimeters of proximal vagina, longer for extensive LVSI or a positive vaginal margin. Consider extra mesorectum or residual uterosacral ligaments. ITV from full and empty bladder, PTV 5 millimeters, with nodal CTV including surgical clips.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Gyne row: Cervical Stage IB1-IIA1 Postoperative EBRT

case: After radical hysterectomy and pelvic radiation for cervical cancer, the pathology showed a close vaginal mucosal margin.
question: How do you boost the vaginal cuff?
answer: A vaginal brachytherapy boost with a segmented cylinder, 6 Gy times 3 fractions prescribed to the vaginal surface, given 1 to 2 fractions per week.
key_points: Indication: close or positive vaginal margin
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Gyne row: Cervical Stage IB1-IIA1 Postoperative EBRT

case: A 48 year old woman has FIGO 2018 stage IIIC1 cervical squamous cell carcinoma and is starting definitive chemoradiation. She asks about immunotherapy.
question: Who gets pembrolizumab with chemoradiation, and how is it dosed?
answer: Pembrolizumab is added for FIGO 2014 IB2 to IIB with node-positive disease, or stage III to IVA regardless of nodes. Concurrent 200 milligrams every 3 weeks times 5, then adjuvant 400 milligrams every 6 weeks for 15 cycles, with weekly cisplatin 40 milligrams per meter squared.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Gyne row: Cervical Stage IB3, IIA2-IVA Definitive CRT

case: A 40 year old woman has a 6 centimeter stage IIB cervical squamous cell carcinoma. Her oncologist asks about induction chemotherapy.
question: What is the induction chemotherapy approach before chemoradiation, and for whom?
answer: For locally advanced disease, FIGO 2008 IB1 node positive, IB2, IIA, IIB, IIIB or IVA, induction weekly carboplatin AUC 2 and paclitaxel 80 milligrams per meter squared for 6 weeks, then standard cisplatin-based chemoradiation and brachytherapy as usual.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Gyne row: Cervical Locally Advanced IC-CRT

case: A woman with stage IIIB cervical cancer and vaginal involvement into the lower third has a PET-avid common iliac node. You are contouring nodes for IMRT.
question: What are your nodal CTV borders and when do you extend them?
answer: Common, external and internal iliac nodes starting at the aortic bifurcation, and presacral nodes down to the S2-S3 interspace, plus 7 millimeters. Add the inguinal nodes for distal vaginal involvement. If para-aortic or high common iliac nodes are involved, extend the superior border to L1-L2 or 3 centimeters above gross disease. Gross nodes get an integrated boost, considering a duodenal PRV.
key_points: Para-aortics: L1-L2 or 3 cm above disease
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Gyne row: Cervical Stage IB3, IIA2-IVA Definitive CRT

case: A woman in week 3 of pelvic chemoradiation for cervical cancer has a platelet count of 70 thousand and an ANC of 1,500.
question: What count thresholds do you use to hold chemotherapy or radiation?
answer: Hold concurrent cisplatin if platelets are under 100 thousand, so cisplatin is held for her, while radiation continues. Hold radiation if platelets fall under 50 thousand and consider holding if ANC is under 1,000. Before brachytherapy, ANC should be above 1,000 and platelets above 50 thousand.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Gyne row: Cervical Stage IB3, IIA2-IVA Definitive CRT

case: A woman with stage IIB cervical cancer has finished pelvic chemoradiation and comes to the OR for her first tandem and ovoid insertion.
question: Walk through the procedure and how you verify the implant.
answer: Under general anesthesia in dorsal lithotomy, do an exam under anesthesia, sound the uterus under ultrasound, dilate the os and suture in a Smit sleeve. Choose the tandem angle, 60 degrees most commonly, place the flange flush to the os, choose the largest ovoids that fit, lock and maximize ovoid separation, then pack posteriorly first and then anteriorly. On fluoroscopy the tandem bisects the ovoids on AP and lateral and points away from the sacrum, the ovoids overlap on lateral, the tandem sits a third to half way between symphysis and sacral promontory, and there is no packing above the ovoids.
key_points: Exam under anesthesia, sound uterus with ultrasound
Tandem angle, flange flush to os
Tandem bisects ovoids, no packing above
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Gyne row: Cervical Definitive CRT, Tandem & Ovoid Procedure

case: A woman with stage IIB cervical cancer has residual bulky, asymmetric parametrial disease after 45 Gy, too far lateral for a tandem and ovoid.
question: When do you use an interstitial implant, and how do you perform it?
answer: Interstitial brachytherapy is used for bulky residual or asymmetric disease in the AP or lateral dimension, or thick upper vaginal involvement. Using a Syed template under anesthesia in dorsal lithotomy, examine noting residual nodularity, place a Foley with contrast in the balloon, insert the vaginal obturator and suture it at the vaginal apex. Insert needles in the 1 centimeter concentric template to cover the initial palpable lesion, uterine and parametrial disease, suture the template to the perineum, place a rectal tube, then CT simulate for planning.
key_points: Bulky, asymmetric, thick upper vaginal disease
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Gyne row: Cervical Definitive CRT, Interstitial Procedure

case: You are contouring an MRI-based cervical brachytherapy plan after 45 Gy of chemoradiation.
question: How do you define the high-risk and intermediate-risk CTVs?
answer: The HR-CTV is residual GTV, the entire cervix, and any presumed extracervical extension including grey zones in the parametria, uterus, vagina, rectum or bladder. The IR-CTV is the HR-CTV plus 5 to 15 millimeters, making sure the initial tumor extent is covered. HR-CTV D90 goal is 80 to 85 Gy EQD2.
key_points: HR-CTV: residual GTV plus whole cervix
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Gyne row: Cervical Definitive CRT, HDR Brachy Boost

case: Two women had hysterectomy for endometrioid adenocarcinoma: a 65 year old with stage IA grade 3 and lymphovascular invasion, and a 55 year old with stage IA grade 2 without risk factors.
question: What are your criteria for vaginal brachytherapy versus pelvic external beam in stage I endometrioid cancer?
answer: Vaginal brachytherapy for stage IA grade 1-2 with a risk factor of age 60 or more or LVSI, stage IA grade 3, or IB grade 1-2. Pelvic EBRT for IA grade 3 with age 70 or more or LVSI, IB grade 2 with age 60 or more or LVSI, or IB grade 3. So the 65 year old with IA grade 3 and LVSI gets pelvic external beam. The 55 year old with IA grade 2 and no risk factors does not need radiation.
key_points: VBT: IA G1-2 with age ≥60 or LVSI
VBT: IA G3 or IB G1-2
EBRT: IA G3 with age ≥70 or LVSI
EBRT: IB G2 with risk factor, or IB G3
No RT: IA G1-2 without risk factors
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Gyne rows: Uterine Endometrioid Stage I VBT and Pelvic EBRT

case: A 62 year old woman has stage IIIC1 endometrioid adenocarcinoma after hysterectomy with cervical stromal involvement and positive pelvic nodes, and will receive pelvic IMRT.
question: What dose and nodal volumes do you use, and when do you extend the field?
answer: 50.4 Gy in 28 fractions, or 45 Gy in 25 if adding a vaginal brachytherapy boost. Nodal CTV covers the lower common, external and internal iliac nodes plus 7 millimeters with a 7 millimeter PTV, adding presacral nodes for cervical involvement and inguinals for distal vaginal involvement. Extended field covers the upper common iliac and para-aortic nodes to 1 to 2 centimeters above the renal vessels. Gross disease is boosted to 60 to 70 Gy as tolerated, and cervical stromal involvement can get a 6 Gy times 3 vaginal surface boost.
key_points: 50.4 Gy in 28 (45 Gy if brachy boost)
Extended field 1-2 cm above renal vessels
Brachy boost 6 Gy x 3 for stromal involvement
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Gyne row: Uterine Endometrioid Stage I Pelvic EBRT

case: A 70 year old woman has uterine serous carcinoma with 30 percent myometrial invasion, negative nodes and negative washings after comprehensive staging.
question: What adjuvant therapy do you recommend?
answer: For invasive serous, clear cell or carcinosarcoma, stage IA through IV, I recommend systemic chemotherapy plus radiation, either vaginal brachytherapy with or without pelvic external beam. Noninvasive IA disease gets vaginal brachytherapy, adding chemotherapy if washings are positive.
key_points: Noninvasive: VBT, chemo if washings positive
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Gyne rows: Uterine Serous/Clear Cell/Carcinosarcoma VBT and VBT + EBRT

case: After radical vulvectomy and inguinofemoral node dissection for vulvar squamous cell carcinoma, a woman has a 3 millimeter margin, 7 millimeter depth, and one 4 millimeter nodal metastasis.
question: What are the indications for adjuvant radiation to the primary and nodes, and for adding chemotherapy?
answer: Primary: close or positive margin under 5 to 8 millimeters, LVSI, depth of invasion over 5 millimeters, and node positivity is a relative indication. Nodes: 2 or more positive nodes, extracapsular extension, clinically or radiographically suspicious nodes, or a single positive sentinel node without completion dissection. Add weekly cisplatin 40 milligrams per meter squared for nodal involvement over 2 millimeters, extracapsular extension, or 2 or more nodes, so she gets chemoradiation.
key_points: Cisplatin if deposit >2 mm, ECE or ≥2 nodes
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Gyne row: Vulvar Postoperative

case: A woman is being simulated for adjuvant vulvar and bilateral groin radiation after vulvectomy and node dissection.
question: Describe your simulation and the inguinal nodal CTV borders.
answer: Supine in frog leg with an empty rectum and full bladder. Wire the vulvar skin borders, scars and any gross disease, with markers on the anus, urethra and clitoris, and use bolus. Groin CTV: lateral to the medial sartorius and rectus femoris, posterior to the anterior vastus medialis, medial to pectineus or 2.5 to 3 centimeters from the vessels, anterior to the anterior sartorius, inferior to the top of the lesser trochanter. Operative bed CTV is the bed plus 2 centimeters, pelvic nodes plus 7 millimeters, PTV 7 millimeters, and confirm dose with TLD on day one.
key_points: Wire vulva, scars; mark anus, urethra, clitoris
Groin inferior: top of lesser trochanter
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Gyne row: Vulvar Postoperative

case: A 70 year old woman has unresectable stage III vulvar squamous cell carcinoma involving the distal urethra, with a 3 centimeter right inguinal node.
question: What are your definitive target volumes?
answer: The primary CTV is the GTV plus 2 centimeters plus the entire vulva, with 2 centimeters into an invaded anorectal, clitoral, urethral or bladder structure and 3 centimeters along the vagina, and a 7 to 10 millimeter PTV, to 64.8 Gy at 1.8 Gy per fraction with weekly cisplatin. The involved node GTV gets a 1 centimeter CTV. Elective nodes get 50.4 Gy in 28 fractions.
key_points: CTV = GTV + 2 cm plus entire vulva
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Gyne row: Vulvar Unresectable Definitive

case: A 65 year old woman has a locally advanced vulvar cancer that could only be resected with loss of the anal sphincter. Her surgeon wants to try neoadjuvant therapy.
question: What is the neoadjuvant chemoradiation approach, and how do you manage based on response?
answer: Cisplatin-based chemoradiation to 57.6 Gy to the primary, with elective nodes to 45 Gy. With a partial response, resect if possible, otherwise give additional chemoradiation. With a clinical complete response, biopsy: if negative, observe; if positive, resect or give more chemoradiation.
key_points: Complete response: biopsy, observe if negative
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Gyne row: Vulvar Unresectable Neoadjuvant

case: A woman with stage II vaginal squamous cell carcinoma has finished 45 Gy of pelvic chemoradiation. Residual disease is 4 millimeters thick on the posterior wall.
question: How do you deliver the brachytherapy boost?
answer: With residual thickness of 5 millimeters or less, an intracavitary vaginal cylinder using the largest cylinder that fits to improve mucosa to tumor dose ratio. HDR 5 to 7 Gy per fraction to 0.5 centimeters depth along the entire vaginal length to 21 to 25 Gy, then an additional 21 to 25 Gy to the tumor with a custom shielded cylinder. Deeper disease over 0.5 centimeters needs an interstitial Syed implant covering the tumor depth to a GTV EQD2 of 75 to 80 Gy. If brachytherapy is not possible, boost the primary to 64 to 70 Gy and gross nodes to 55 to 66 Gy.
key_points: 21-25 Gy to entire vagina, then shielded boost
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Gyne row: Vaginal Brachy + EBRT

case: A 55 year old man has a 5 centimeter high grade sarcoma confined to the subcutaneous tissue of the back, superficial to the fascia, planned for pre-operative radiation.
question: How do your target volumes differ for a subcutaneous tumor?
answer: GTV is the tumor on T1 contrast MRI. Because it is not in a muscle compartment, the CTV is a 3 to 4 centimeter circumferential margin with only 0.5 to 1 centimeter into the underlying uninvolved muscle, including T2 peritumoral edema and the biopsy tract when feasible. PTV is 5 millimeters, cropped 3 to 5 millimeters under the skin, to 50 Gy in 25 fractions, keeping the skin strip V20 under 50 percent.
key_points: Include T2 edema and biopsy tract
PTV 5 mm, cropped 3-5 mm from skin
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Sarcoma row: Extremity/Body Wall Pre-Op

case: A woman had wide excision of a subcutaneous high grade sarcoma of the arm without pre-operative radiation and is referred for post-operative radiation.
question: What is your initial post-operative CTV for a subcutaneous tumor?
answer: CTV1 is the tumor bed, defined by clips and the pre-operative MRI, plus a 3 to 4 centimeter circumferential margin, extending 0.5 to 1 centimeter into uninvolved muscle, plus the operative field, scar and drain sites when feasible, with a 5 millimeter PTV to 50 Gy in 25 fractions. The boost CTV2 is the bed plus 1.5 to 2 centimeters circumferentially and 0.5 centimeters into muscle, to 60 Gy, or 66 Gy for R1.
key_points: Bed from clips and pre-op MRI
Include scar, operative field, drain sites
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Sarcoma row: Extremity/Body Wall Post-Op

case: A 60 year old woman has a 12 centimeter retroperitoneal liposarcoma, and the tumor board recommends pre-operative radiation.
question: How do you modify the CTV expansion at different tissue interfaces?
answer: With a 4D CT and iGTV, the CTV is the iGTV plus 1.5 centimeters except at interfaces: 0 millimeters into retroperitoneal compartment boundaries, bone, liver and kidney, 5 millimeters into bowel and air cavities, and 3 to 5 millimeters under the skin. If the tumor extends into the inguinal canal, expand 3 centimeters inferiorly. PTV is 5 millimeters, 50 Gy in 25 fractions with IMRT.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Sarcoma row: RP Pre-Op

case: At resection of an extremity sarcoma, the surgeon asks if you can place brachytherapy catheters in the tumor bed.
question: What target and doses do you use for LDR brachytherapy, alone or with external beam?
answer: The CTV is the tumor bed and areas at risk, expanding the surgical bed by 2 centimeters cranio-caudally and 1 to 2 centimeters laterally per ABS. LDR monotherapy is 45 to 50 Gy over 4 to 6 days at 0.45 to 0.5 Gy per hour. Combined with external beam, the LDR boost is 15 to 25 Gy over 2 to 4 days. For retroperitoneal sarcoma after pre-op radiation, an intraoperative boost is 10 to 15 Gy.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Sarcoma rows: Extremity IORT and RP IORT

case: A 26-year-old with early stage classical Hodgkin lymphoma has finished chemotherapy and is referred for consolidative involved-site radiation.
question: How do you define your target volumes for involved-site radiation, and how does that differ from involved-node radiation?
answer: Fuse the pre-chemotherapy PET-CT to the post-chemotherapy simulation CT. GTV is the pre-chemo involved nodes on CT and PET; CTV is the post-chemo tissue that originally contained lymphoma, accounting for shrinkage and sparing uninvolved organs; add an ITV if there is motion, then a PTV margin depending on site and technique. Involved-node RT is ISRT with optimal imaging, meaning a pre-chemo PET-CT acquired in the treatment position. Start RT about 3 to 4 weeks after chemo.
key_points: INRT needs pre-chemo PET in treatment position
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Heme row: Hodgkins Lymphoma, Classic, Stage IA/IIA Favorable

case: A 34-year-old has classical Hodgkin lymphoma of the neck and mediastinum, stage IIA.
question: What NCCN factors make early stage Hodgkin lymphoma unfavorable?
answer: NCCN unfavorable factors are ESR of 50 or more or any B symptoms, a mediastinal mass ratio over 0.33, more than 3 nodal sites, and bulky disease over 10 centimeters.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Heme row: Hodgkins Lymphoma, Classic, Stage I/II Unfavorable

case: A 29-year-old has stage IIA classical Hodgkin lymphoma with a mediastinal mass ratio of 0.4. Interim PET after 2 cycles of ABVD is Deauville 3.
question: What is your management, and what are alternative systemic approaches?
answer: This is early stage unfavorable disease. With Deauville 1 to 3, give 2 more cycles of ABVD, or AVD for 4, followed by ISRT to 30 Gy in 15 fractions. If Deauville 4 to 5, 2 more cycles of ABVD or BrECADD, biopsy a Deauville 5, then ISRT 30 Gy. Alternatives are nivolumab-AVD or brentuximab-AVD for 4 cycles plus ISRT 30 Gy, or BrECADD for 4 to 6 cycles with or without ISRT.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Heme row: Hodgkins Lymphoma, Classic, Stage I/II Unfavorable

case: A 40-year-old has stage IVB classical Hodgkin lymphoma with nodal disease above and below the diaphragm and lung involvement.
question: What is your recommended treatment and when is radiation used?
answer: Preferred options are nivolumab-AVD for 6 cycles, or BrECADD for 2 cycles with interim PET: Deauville 1 to 3 gets 2 more cycles, Deauville 4 to 5 is biopsied and if negative gets 4 more. Radiation, ISRT to 30 Gy in 15 fractions, is reserved for residual Deauville 4 to 5 sites with negative biopsy at end of therapy. ABVD then AVD is less preferred.
key_points: ISRT only for residual PET-positive sites
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Heme row: Hodgkins Lymphoma, Classic, Stage III/IV

case: A 35-year-old has stage IA nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma in a single neck node and opts for radiation alone.
question: How do you design the target and what dose do you use?
answer: Options are ISRT or observation. With radiation alone, the CTV is more generous than after chemo: the GTV plus at least the adjacent lymph nodes in that site with a 3 to 5 centimeter margin, because microscopic disease is not addressed by chemotherapy. Dose is 30 Gy in 15 fractions, up to 36 Gy if bulky.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Heme row: Hodgkins Lymphoma, NLP-HL, Stage IA/IIA

case: A 42-year-old has nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, stage IIB with B symptoms.
question: How does management differ from stage IA disease, and what about advanced stage?
answer: Stage IA or IIA bulky disease and stage IB or IIB get chemotherapy plus rituximab followed by ISRT to 30 Gy in 15 fractions. Stage III to IV gets chemotherapy plus rituximab with or without ISRT, or rituximab alone.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Heme rows: Hodgkins Lymphoma, NLP-HL, Stage IA/IIA bulky, IB/IIB, III-IV

case: A patient with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is being considered for radiation in several scenarios.
question: What doses do you use for DLBCL with radiation alone, partial response, refractory disease, around transplant, and for testicular prophylaxis?
answer: Radiation alone is 40 Gy. Partial response is 36 to 50 Gy and refractory disease 40 to 55 Gy. Combined with stem cell transplant, 20 to 36 Gy. Prophylactic contralateral testis RT is 25 to 30 Gy. Complete response consolidation is 20 to 36 Gy, with 20 Gy only for DLBCL based on two phase II dose-reduction trials.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Heme row: Aggressive B-Cell Lymphoma, DLBCL, Stage I-II smIPI 0-1

case: A 58-year-old has stage II diffuse large B-cell lymphoma with a 9 centimeter mediastinal mass, stage-modified IPI 1.
question: What is your management and where does radiation fit?
answer: Bulky disease over 7.5 centimeters is treated like higher-risk disease: R-CHOP for 3 cycles then PET. With Deauville 1 to 3, 3 more cycles of R-CHOP with or without ISRT to the bulky site; Deauville 4, 3 more cycles with or without ISRT and biopsy if still positive; Deauville 5 gets a biopsy. The same approach applies to stage I-II with smIPI over 1 and stage III-IV.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Heme rows: Aggressive B-Cell Lymphoma, DLBCL, Bulky >7.5cm and smIPI>1 / Stage III-IV

case: A 55-year-old has a grade 1 to 2 follicular lymphoma confined to a single inguinal node, stage IA.
question: What is your recommended treatment and dose?
answer: Involved-site radiation alone is preferred for stage I or contiguous stage II follicular lymphoma, to 24 to 30 Gy. Non-contiguous stage II should get at least rituximab, with or without CHOP, with or without ISRT.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Heme row: Indolent B-Cell Lymphoma, Follicular, Definitive

case: A 72-year-old with stage IV follicular lymphoma has a symptomatic, enlarging axillary mass.
question: What are the FLIPI factors, and what radiation would you offer for palliation?
answer: FLIPI factors are age 60 or older, stage III or IV, hemoglobin under 12, LDH above normal, and 5 or more nodal sites. For palliation, low-dose ISRT to 4 Gy, given as 2 Gy times 2 or a single 4 Gy fraction.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Heme row: Indolent B-Cell Lymphoma, Follicular, Palliative

case: A 66-year-old has stage IE gastric MALT lymphoma on endoscopic biopsy.
question: Who goes straight to radiation, and what is the role of H. pylori therapy?
answer: Stage I to II gastric MALT that is H. pylori negative or carries t(11;18) goes to radiation upfront. H. pylori positive patients get eradication with quadruple therapy: PPI, bismuth subsalicylate, tetracycline and metronidazole. RT is for refractory disease after antibiotics, trying second-line antibiotics first when appropriate or, if asymptomatic, repeating endoscopy and biopsy at 3 months. Stage II2 or higher symptomatic disease gets palliative RT.
key_points: H. pylori negative goes to RT
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Heme rows: Marginal Zone Lymphoma, Gastric MALT, Definitive and Palliative

case: A 70-year-old with H. pylori negative stage IE gastric MALT lymphoma is referred for definitive radiation.
question: What is your target and dose, and why that fractionation?
answer: The CTV is the entire stomach. Dose is 24 Gy in 16 fractions at 1.5 Gy per fraction, using the smaller fraction size to minimize acute GI toxicity.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Heme row: Marginal Zone Lymphoma, Gastric MALT, Definitive

case: A 64-year-old has non-bulky stage II mantle cell lymphoma of the neck.
question: What are your treatment options and doses?
answer: ISRT alone, or a less aggressive induction such as R-CHOP with or without ISRT. Radiation alone is 36 Gy; after chemo, 24 to 30 Gy for complete response and 36 Gy for partial response.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Heme row: B-Cell Lymphoma, Mantle Cell, Stage I or II nonbulky

case: A 30-year-old with acute leukemia is going to allogeneic stem cell transplant and the team asks about total body irradiation.
question: What are your myeloablative and nonmyeloablative TBI doses?
answer: Myeloablative TBI is 12 Gy in 6 to 8 fractions given twice daily. Reduced-intensity or nonmyeloablative conditioning is 2 to 4 Gy in 1 to 2 fractions.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Heme rows: TBI, Myeloablative and Conditioning

case: A 58-year-old with widespread thick-plaque and tumor-stage mycosis fungoides is referred for full-dose total skin electron therapy.
question: Describe your dose and technique.
answer: 36 Gy total, treating 4 days a week with a 1 week break after week 4; it can be lowered to 12 Gy. Prescribe 26 Gy to 4 millimeters depth so the surface gets 31 to 36 Gy. Use six positions, AP and both posterior obliques on day 1 and PA and both anterior obliques on day 2, each with split fields for homogeneity. Use eye and nail shields, and patch underdosed areas like scalp, soles, inframammary folds, perineum and inner thighs.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Heme row: Mycosis Fungoides, TSEBT

case: A 50-year-old presents with a single mycosis fungoides plaque on the thigh with no other skin disease.
question: What dose and margin do you use?
answer: Unilesional mycosis fungoides is treated definitively to 24 to 30 Gy in 12 to 15 fractions, targeting the lesion plus a 10 to 15 millimeter margin.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Heme row: Mycosis Fungoides, Individual plaque, Definitive

case: A 68-year-old with widespread mycosis fungoides has a symptomatic, itchy ulcerated plaque on the forearm.
question: What palliative regimen would you use?
answer: Local electron or photon field to the lesion plus 10 to 15 millimeters, with 8 Gy in 2 fractions or 12 Gy in 3 fractions.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Heme row: Mycosis Fungoides, Individual plaque, Palliative

case: A 72-year-old with stage I extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type, involving the unilateral anterior nasal cavity, is unfit for chemotherapy.
question: What dose do you use and how do you define the CTV?
answer: Radiation alone to 50 Gy, NCCN 50 to 55 Gy. GTV from endoscopy, MRI, CT and PET. For unilateral anterior or mid nasal cavity disease, the CTV includes both nasal cavities, the ipsilateral maxillary sinus and bilateral anterior ethmoids. Add both maxillary sinuses for bilateral nasal disease, the nasopharynx for posterior nasal involvement, and posterior ethmoids if anterior ethmoids are involved, plus all involved sinuses, soft tissue extension and involved nodes. No elective nodal irradiation.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Heme row: Extranodal NK/T, RT alone

case: A 78-year-old medically inoperable patient has a 1.8 centimeter peripheral right upper lobe adenocarcinoma, node negative. A second patient has a similar tumor abutting the chest wall.
question: What SBRT dose regimens do you use for each?
answer: For a peripheral tumor, 54 Gy in 3 fractions given every other day, or 34 Gy in a single fraction. For a peripheral tumor near the chest wall, 50 Gy in 5 daily fractions to limit chest wall toxicity. Both are planned with IMRT on a 4D CT and treated with daily kV and cone beam CT.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Thoracic rows: Lung NSCLC Early Stage, Peripheral SBRT and Peripheral Near Chest Wall SBRT

case: A 74-year-old has a 2 centimeter node-negative non-small cell lung cancer abutting the proximal bronchial tree, an ultracentral tumor.
question: How do you simulate and what dose do you prescribe?
answer: Supine with arms up on an immobilization board with upper and lower vacuum bags, 4D CT with IV contrast. GTV on the 50 percent phase or average, iGTV as the union across phases, then PTV per standard SBRT margins. Prescribe 60 Gy in 8 fractions or 70 Gy in 10 fractions with IMRT and daily cone beam CT.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Thoracic row: Lung NSCLC Early Stage, UltraCentral SBRT

case: A 61-year-old with unresectable stage IIIB non-small cell lung cancer will receive definitive chemoradiation to 60 Gy.
question: Which concurrent chemotherapy regimens and doses do you use, and what is the adjuvant therapy?
answer: Weekly carboplatin AUC 2 with paclitaxel 45 to 50 milligrams per meter squared, or cisplatin 50 milligrams per meter squared on days 1, 8, 29 and 36 with etoposide 50 milligrams per meter squared days 1 to 5 and 29 to 33. Both are acceptable for squamous and nonsquamous histology. Then durvalumab 1500 milligrams every 4 weeks for 12 months, or osimertinib 80 milligrams daily until progression for EGFR-mutant disease.
key_points: durvalumab 1500 mg q4 weeks x12 months
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Thoracic row: Lung NSCLC Locally Advanced, Definitive CRT

case: You are planning 60 Gy in 30 fractions for locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer.
question: What are your lung, heart and esophagus constraints?
answer: Lung V20 at or below 35 to 40 percent and mean lung dose at or below 20 Gy. Heart V40 at or below 20 percent and mean at or below 20 Gy. Esophagus mean at or below 34 Gy, max at or below 105 percent of prescription, V60 at or below 17 percent, and spare the contralateral esophagus when possible.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Thoracic row: Lung NSCLC Locally Advanced, Definitive CRT (OAR constraints)

case: A patient with stage IIIA non-small cell lung cancer has a 1.3 centimeter right paratracheal node that is not PET avid and was not biopsied.
question: How do you decide which nodes to include in the gross nodal target?
answer: GTVn includes nodes over 1 centimeter in short axis on CT, or SUV over 3, or biopsy positive, contoured on the 50 percent phase or average and summed across all phases into an iGTV. This node qualifies by size. The CTV expands the iGTV but is cropped at barriers of spread such as muscle, bronchial tree, uninvolved vessels and heart.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Thoracic row: Lung NSCLC Locally Advanced, Definitive CRT (Volume Description)

case: A patient had lobectomy with mediastinal dissection showing pN2 disease with extranodal extension, and you decide on postoperative radiation.
question: Describe your postoperative target volumes.
answer: Per the Lung ART protocol, the resected CTV includes the bronchial stump, involved nodal stations based on pathology and pre-chemo extent, the ipsilateral hilum at station 10, and the mediastinal pleura adjacent to the resected bed. Expand 1 centimeter excluding vertebral body, include the stations above and below involved stations and any between non-contiguous stations. PTV is 5 millimeters radially and 1 centimeter superior-inferior. With ENE or a positive margin, dose is 54 to 60 Gy.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Thoracic row: Lung NSCLC Locally Advanced, Postop CRT

case: A patient with limited stage small cell lung cancer is starting chemoradiation but cannot come in twice daily.
question: What are your requirements for twice-daily treatment and your alternatives?
answer: Twice-daily 45 Gy in 1.5 Gy fractions requires an interfraction interval of at least 6 hours. If the patient declines twice daily, options are 66 Gy in 33 once-daily fractions or a hypofractionated 40 Gy in 15 fractions. Volumes are the same as for NSCLC chemoradiation.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Thoracic row: Lung SCLC LS, CRT

case: A patient with limited stage small cell lung cancer in complete response is getting prophylactic cranial irradiation with a 3D technique.
question: Describe your simulation, field borders and spinal cord constraint.
answer: Supine, head neutral, thermoplastic mask. Isocenter midplane with opposed laterals, collimator rotated to block the anterior orbit and tissues anterior to the skull base. Borders: 2 centimeters flash superiorly and posteriorly, inferior at the bottom of C1, anteriorly blocking from flash to the front of C1 to spare lens and parotid. 25 Gy in 10 fractions, cord max 36 to 41 Gy, with kV imaging daily.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Thoracic row: Lung SCLC LS, PCI

case: A patient is about to start prophylactic cranial irradiation and you recommend memantine for neurocognitive protection.
question: How do you dose memantine?
answer: Titrate up: 5 milligrams daily in week 1, 5 milligrams twice daily in week 2, 10 milligrams in the morning and 5 in the evening in week 3, then 10 milligrams twice daily from week 4 through week 24.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Thoracic row: Lung SCLC LS, PCI (memantine)

case: A 57-year-old has an unresectable thymoma invading the great vessels.
question: What is your recommended treatment, including chemotherapy doses?
answer: Definitive radiation to 60 Gy in 30 fractions, considering up to 70 Gy, with consideration of concurrent carboplatin AUC 6 and paclitaxel 200 milligrams per meter squared on day 1 every 3 weeks. Target the gross tumor with an ITV from 4D CT and a 5 millimeter PTV.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Thoracic row: Thymoma, Unresectable

case: A patient with oligometastatic non-small cell lung cancer has a good response to systemic therapy with residual disease in the primary.
question: How do you approach consolidative thoracic radiation?
answer: Simulate as for definitive lung RT, supine arms up with 4D CT and IV contrast. Treat residual disease only, not the original extent, choosing SBRT or conventionally fractionated RT with or without chemotherapy depending on the residual extent.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Thoracic row: Lung NSCLC Oligometastatic, Consolidative Thoracic

case: A 58-year-old man with T2 N1 p16-positive tonsil cancer will get definitive IMRT.
question: Describe your simulation and image guidance.
answer: Supine with a head rest and the neck extended, IV contrast, and a 5-point thermoplastic mask covering head, neck and shoulders. A bite block or mouth guard, and instruct him not to swallow during scans and treatment. Daily kV or cone beam CT.
key_points: Daily kV or cone beam CT
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Oropharynx early stage, Definitive

case: A 60-year-old with T2 N0 squamous cell carcinoma of the tonsil, no chemotherapy planned, treated with radiation alone.
question: What dose and fractionation, and how do you build your gross and elective target volumes?
answer: 66 Gy in 30 fractions to gross disease and 54 Gy in 30 fractions electively. GTV is gross primary and suspicious nodes, meaning over 1 centimeter, necrotic, enhancing or FDG-avid; CTV is GTV plus 5 millimeters and PTV a further 5 millimeters. Subclinical primary CTV is GTV plus 10 millimeters, plus the elective nodes.
key_points: Suspicious node over 1 cm, necrotic, FDG-avid
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Oropharynx early stage, Definitive

case: A 64-year-old with a T1 N1 well-lateralized tonsil squamous cell carcinoma planned for definitive IMRT.
question: Which elective nodal levels do you cover, and when can you treat the ipsilateral neck only?
answer: Standard is bilateral levels II to IV and retropharyngeal VIIa. Ipsilateral-only is reasonable for T1 to T2, N0 to N1 well-lateralized tonsil cancers with 1 centimeter or less of invasion into the soft palate or base of tongue. Add level V for node positive or tonsil and base of tongue, IB for oral cavity extension or anterior level II, IVb if IVa is involved, and retrostyloid VIIb for bulky upper level II.
key_points: Bilateral II to IV plus retropharyngeal
Ipsilateral if T1-2 N0-1 lateralized tonsil
1 cm or less into palate or base of tongue
VIIb for bulky upper level II
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Oropharynx early stage, Definitive

case: A 55-year-old with an oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma planned for definitive IMRT.
question: How does your subclinical primary CTV differ for a tonsil, base of tongue, or soft palate primary?
answer: Tonsil: include the pterygoid plates if locally advanced and the ipsilateral retromolar trigone if it spreads anterolaterally along the constrictor. Base of tongue: the glossotonsillar sulcus, vallecula and pre-epiglottic space. Soft palate: the entire soft palate, upper tonsillar pillars and fossa, and adjacent nasopharynx up to the pterygopalatine fossa. Pharyngeal wall primaries need generous superior and inferior margins for skip lesions.
key_points: Base of tongue: vallecula, pre-epiglottic space
Soft palate: entire palate to pterygopalatine fossa
Pharyngeal wall: generous for skip lesions
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Oropharynx early stage, Definitive

case: A 66-year-old with T3 N2 oropharyngeal cancer planned for definitive chemoradiation, but with chronic kidney disease and hearing loss.
question: What is your standard regimen, and what are the alternatives if she is cisplatin ineligible or not a chemo candidate?
answer: Standard is 70 Gy in 35 fractions with 56 Gy in 35 electively, concurrent with cisplatin 100 milligrams per meter squared on weeks 1, 4 and 7, or 40 weekly. Category 1 alternative is carboplatin with infusional 5-FU. If cisplatin ineligible, docetaxel or cetuximab. If not a chemo candidate, altered fractionation radiation alone.
key_points: Docetaxel or cetuximab if cisplatin ineligible
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Oropharynx locally advanced, Definitive

case: Definitive IMRT for an oropharyngeal cancer; you are reviewing the plan.
question: Beyond parotids and cord, what are your limits for the brainstem, cord PRV, optic structures, TMJ, lips and glottis?
answer: Brainstem PRV 0.03 cc 54 to 58 Gy. Spinal cord max 45 Gy with the cord plus 5 millimeter PRV max 48 Gy. Chiasm, optic nerves and eyes under 55 Gy to 0.03 cc. TMJ 0.03 cc under 70 to 75 Gy. Lips mean under 20 Gy, glottis mean under 45 Gy and larynx mean under 35 Gy.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Oropharynx early stage, Definitive (constraint metrics)

case: A 50-year-old with p16-positive tonsil cancer after TORS and neck dissection: pT2, margins 2 millimeters, 3 positive ipsilateral nodes, 0.5 millimeter extranodal extension.
question: Is he a candidate for de-escalated adjuvant radiation, and what dose?
answer: Yes, per ECOG 3311 criteria: p16 positive, 4 or fewer positive nodes, T1 to T2 resected to negative or close margins under 3 millimeters, N1 to N2 without bilateral disease, and extranodal extension 1 millimeter or less. He could receive 50 Gy in 25 fractions instead of 60. Note E3311 defined a positive margin as under 1 millimeter.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Oropharynx Postop

case: Post-op oropharynx cancer with a positive margin and extranodal extension in a level II node.
question: How do you build the postoperative CTVs?
answer: 66 Gy to the region of the positive margin or extranodal extension plus 10 millimeters. 60 Gy to the postoperative bed plus 10 to 15 millimeters, and to the preoperative involved nodes plus 10 millimeters together with the involved nodal levels. Lower dose to undissected or low-risk dissected elective levels. Consider extra superior margin for oral cavity and superior-inferior for larynx.
key_points: 66 Gy to margin or ENE region
60 Gy to bed plus 10 to 15 mm
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Oropharynx Postop

case: A patient with oral cavity cancer is coming for IMRT simulation.
question: How does your simulation differ from oropharynx, specifically the bite block?
answer: Supine, neck extended, IV contrast, 5-point mask. The bite block is used to depress the tongue, protrude the lower lip and elevate the palate, displacing uninvolved oral structures away from the target, for example sparing the palate in an oral tongue primary.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Oral Cavity Postop

case: A 70-year-old after resection of a pT3 N1 buccal mucosa squamous cell carcinoma with perineural invasion.
question: What are your primary and nodal CTVs?
answer: For buccal mucosa, retromolar trigone, hard palate or gingiva, CTVp is the tumor bed plus 10 to 15 millimeters, not the entire subsite. Nodes: ipsilateral levels I to IV, add level V if node positive and contralateral if contralateral nodes are involved. For buccal mucosa specifically, include the ipsilateral buccofacial level IX nodes.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Oral Cavity Postop

case: A 76-year-old with unresectable T4a N1 squamous cell carcinoma of the lower alveolar ridge receiving definitive chemoradiation.
question: What doses and target volumes do you use, and when can you treat one side of the neck?
answer: 70 Gy in 35 fractions to GTV plus 5 millimeters and 56 Gy in 35 electively, with cisplatin. The subclinical primary CTV is GTV plus 10 millimeters plus the entire anatomic subsite. Elective nodes are bilateral I to IVa and V; unilateral is acceptable for N0 to N2a lateralized alveolar ridge, lateral floor of mouth and buccal tumors. Add Ia for anterior tongue and lower lip; V can be omitted if only I or II involved.
key_points: GTV plus 10 mm plus entire subsite
Bilateral I to IVa and V
Unilateral if lateralized N0 to N2a
Ia for anterior tongue, lower lip
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Oral Cavity Definitive, Unresectable

case: A 40-year-old has a T1 N0 nasopharyngeal carcinoma on MRI and PET.
question: Does she need chemotherapy, and which nodal levels do you electively treat?
answer: No chemotherapy for T1 to T2 N0, unless T2 N0 with high risk features such as bulky tumor or high plasma EBV DNA. Radiation alone with IMRT. For T1 N0, elective levels II, III, VA and retropharyngeal and retrostyloid VII, omitting levels IV and VB in the node negative neck.
key_points: Unless bulky or high EBV DNA
Omit IV and VB for N0
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Nasopharyngeal early stage, Definitive

case: A 48-year-old with T3 N1 nasopharyngeal carcinoma, left neck nodes only, after induction chemotherapy.
question: How do you define the elective nodal CTV?
answer: Bilateral levels IB to V with retropharyngeal VIIa and retrostyloid VIIb. Omit levels IV and VB on the node negative side. Include IB if the submandibular gland is involved, a structure draining to IB is involved, or level II is involved. Add IVb if III or IVa are involved, and VC if VA or VB are involved.
key_points: Bilateral IB to V plus VIIa and VIIb
Omit IV and VB on N0 side
IB if submandibular or level II involved
IVb if III or IVa involved
VC if VA or VB involved
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Nasopharyngeal locally advanced, Definitive

case: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma confined to the left nasopharynx, not crossing midline on MRI, compared to a T4 tumor with skull base invasion.
question: How does the low-risk primary CTV change with T stage and lateralization?
answer: For T1 to T2, cover the inferior half of the sphenoid sinus, the anterior third of the clivus, and omit the cavernous sinus. For T3 to T4 with skull base invasion, cover the whole sphenoid sinus and clivus and the whole ipsilateral cavernous sinus. Parapharyngeal space, foramina ovale, rotundum and lacerum, pterygoid process and pterygopalatine fossa are bilateral, but ipsilateral for well lateralized tumors.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Nasopharyngeal locally advanced, Definitive

case: A 66-year-old with carcinoma in situ of the left true vocal cord, involving the anterior commissure, choosing radiation.
question: What dose and how do you simulate?
answer: 60.75 Gy in 27 fractions at 2.25 Gy per fraction. Supine, neck extended, IV contrast, 5-point mask, with a shoulder pull board to lower the shoulders out of the beam path. No swallowing during simulation and treatment, and bolus because of anterior commissure involvement. Daily kV or cone beam CT.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Larynx Glottic, TisN0

case: A 70-year-old with T1a N0 glottic cancer treated with 3D opposed laterals.
question: Describe your field borders and isocenter.
answer: Isocenter at the true vocal cords, field about 5 by 5 to 6 by 6 centimeters. Superior at the top of the thyroid cartilage, inferior at the bottom of the cricoid cartilage, anterior flash, and posterior at the anterior margin of the vertebral body. Wedges 15 to 30 degrees with heels anterior, 5 millimeter bolus if anterior commissure involved, and a couch kick for broad shoulders.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Larynx Glottic, T1N0

case: A 68-year-old with T2 N0 glottic cancer with supraglottic extension, treated with 3D opposed laterals.
question: How do your field borders differ from a T1 glottic cancer?
answer: Fields enlarge: superior border 1 centimeter above the top of the thyroid cartilage, anterior flash about 1 centimeter beyond skin, and inferior border one tracheal ring below the cricoid or as low as possible without treating the shoulders. Posterior stays at the anterior vertebral body. Dose 65.25 Gy in 29 fractions at 2.25.
key_points: Inferior one tracheal ring below cricoid
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Larynx Glottic, T2N0

case: A singer with T1 glottic cancer will be treated with carotid-sparing IMRT.
question: Define your CTV and PTV.
answer: GTV is visible disease on laryngoscopy. CTV is the entire larynx: the glottis including true cords and anterior and posterior commissures, the supraglottis including false cords and arytenoids up to the top of the thyroid notch, and subglottis to the cricoid cartilage, or first tracheal ring for T2. Paraglottic space and thyroid cartilage if at risk, and at least 2 centimeters craniocaudally. PTV is CTV plus 3 to 5 millimeters.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Larynx Glottic, T1N0

case: A 62-year-old with T3 N1 supraglottic cancer, vocal cord fixed, no cartilage invasion, wanting to keep his larynx.
question: Is he a larynx preservation candidate, and what are your elective volumes?
answer: Yes; definitive chemoradiation for T3 or node positive disease, 70 Gy in 35 with cisplatin. T4a with thyroid cartilage invasion or significant soft tissue extension should get laryngectomy. Elective 56 Gy covers the entire larynx and bilateral II to IVa, adding IB for gross nodes, V for node positive, IVb if IVa involved, VIb for subglottic extension, VIIa for posterior pharyngeal wall or base of tongue, and VIIb for bulky nodes.
key_points: Chemoradiation for T3 or N positive
VIIa for pharyngeal wall or tongue base
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Larynx locally advanced, Definitive

case: After total laryngectomy for a pT4a N2b laryngeal cancer with subglottic extension and close margins.
question: What are your indications for adjuvant radiation, and what special areas must your CTV include?
answer: Indications include pT3 to T4, close margins, subglottic extension, pN2 to N3, PNI and LVI, with chemotherapy for positive margins or ENE. The 60 Gy CTV includes the operative bed, scar and stoma plus 10 to 15 millimeters, and involved nodal levels. Electively cover level VI and VII when there is subglottic extension or a stoma.
key_points: Bed and scar plus 10 to 15 mm
Level VI and VII for subglottic or stoma
Chemo for margin positive or ENE
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Larynx Postoperative

case: Post-op radiation after superficial parotidectomy for a high grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma with perineural invasion.
question: Describe the borders of your parotid bed CTV and your elective nodal levels.
answer: The parotid bed CTV spans the masseter anteriorly to the mastoid bone posteriorly, soft tissue of the neck laterally, and the styloid process medially at depth, extending to the parapharyngeal fat depending on gland extent. 60 Gy to the bed. Electively treat the ipsilateral node negative levels IB to IV plus the parotid level VIII nodes, and level V if node positive.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Salivary Gland Postoperative

case: Salivary gland carcinoma with perineural invasion after resection: one patient with a parotid primary, one with a submandibular adenoid cystic carcinoma.
question: Which nerves do you trace in each case?
answer: Parotid: the facial nerve, glossopharyngeal nerve and mandibular division of the trigeminal, V3, possibly back to Meckel's cave. Submandibular or sublingual: the lingual nerve, a branch of V, and the hypoglossal nerve, with or without the facial nerve, extending to Meckel's cave especially for adenoid cystic carcinoma.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Salivary Gland Postoperative

case: A 60-year-old with squamous cell carcinoma in a left level II node, EBV negative and p16 negative, no primary found after full workup.
question: Which mucosal sites do you include, and how does this change with viral status?
answer: Putative mucosal sites get about 56 Gy, higher for particularly suspicious areas. EBV positive: the nasopharynx. p16 positive: the oropharynx, with or without nasopharynx, but not larynx, hypopharynx or oral cavity. When both negative, as here, treat the pharyngeal axis: nasopharynx, oropharynx and hypopharynx. The larynx and hypopharynx volume runs from the hyoid to the bottom of the cricoid.
key_points: Not larynx or oral cavity if p16
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Unknown Primary, Definitive

case: A 57-year-old with p16-positive unknown primary had a neck dissection: 3 positive nodes, one with extranodal extension.
question: What adjuvant therapy and doses do you recommend?
answer: Adjuvant radiation is indicated for N1 to N3; observation can be considered for N1 without extranodal extension. With extranodal extension, add concurrent cisplatin, and consider it for N2 to N3. 66 Gy to the ENE region plus 10 millimeters, 60 Gy to the preoperative nodes plus 10 millimeters and involved levels, and lower dose to elective nodal and mucosal sites.
key_points: 66 Gy to ENE region plus 10 mm
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Unknown Primary, Postop (LND)

case: A 69-year-old with unresected anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, no distant metastases, for definitive radiation.
question: What doses and targets do you use?
answer: 70 Gy in 35 fractions to the gross primary and nodes with CTV GTV plus 5 millimeters. 56 Gy in 35 to the subclinical volume, CTVp plus 5 millimeters plus the tracheoesophageal groove, and bilateral elective nodal levels II through VII.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Thyroid Intact, Definitive (Anaplastic)

case: A thyroidectomy specimen: one patient with papillary, one with medullary, one with anaplastic carcinoma.
question: When is postoperative external beam radiation indicated for each histology?
answer: Anaplastic: after R0 or R1 resection. Papillary or follicular: R1 or unresectable residual disease unlikely to respond to radioiodine, or high risk for residual such as age 55 or older, extrathyroidal extension, or poorly differentiated histology. Medullary: R1 or persistently elevated calcitonin or CEA. Doses follow standard postop levels of 66, 60 and 54 Gy, including any tracheostomy to the skin.
key_points: Papillary: R1 or residual not RAI responsive
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Thyroid Postop, EBRT

case: A 45-year-old after total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid cancer is planned for radioactive iodine remnant ablation.
question: How do you prepare her?
answer: Raise TSH above 30 by hormone withdrawal, endogenous hormone half-life 4 to 6 weeks. Iodine restricted diet for 7 to 14 days, holding supplements. Confirm no recent iodinated contrast, no amiodarone in the last year, and a negative pregnancy test. Consider a diagnostic 1 to 2 millicurie I-131 scan, within 48 to 72 hours of therapy to avoid stunning.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Thyroid RAI

case: Three patients with differentiated thyroid cancer after thyroidectomy: low-risk remnant, higher risk pathology, and known metastatic disease.
question: What I-131 activities do you give in each setting?
answer: Remnant ablation 30 to 50 millicuries. Adjuvant therapy for higher likelihood of residual disease, 75 to 150 millicuries. Proven unresectable or metastatic disease, 100 to 200 millicuries.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), H&N row: Thyroid RAI

case: An 82-year-old with a 7 millimeter basal cell carcinoma of the nasal ala asks whether radiation is reasonable instead of surgery.
question: When is definitive radiation favored for keratinocyte skin cancers?
answer: For non-surgical candidates and where surgery would compromise function or cosmesis: central face lesions over 5 millimeters such as the nasal ala, eyelids and nasal tip, the lip commissure, and lesions over 2 centimeters on the ears, forehead or scalp. Yes, she is a reasonable candidate.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Skin row: SCC Intact

case: A 79-year-old with a 2.5 centimeter squamous cell carcinoma of the forehead, clinically node negative, treated definitively.
question: What dose fractionation options do you have, and what about nerves and nodes?
answer: 70 Gy in 35 fractions, or hypofractionated 55 Gy in 20 fractions; lesions under 2 centimeters can get 60 Gy in 30. Clinically at-risk nerves are included as a perineural CTV, and elective nodes for clinically node negative patients at risk get about 50 Gy. Use an eye shield for eyelid lesions.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Skin row: SCC Intact

case: A 74-year-old with a borderline resectable cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the scalp with in-transit disease.
question: What is the role of systemic therapy?
answer: Concurrent chemotherapy is only a conditional recommendation per ASTRO for locally advanced disease. Consider neoadjuvant cemiplimab for borderline resectable disease, high anticipated surgical morbidity, in-transit disease, N3 disease, or extracapsular extension.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Skin row: SCC Intact

case: A 76-year-old after excision of a cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma of the cheek with a positive margin and parotid and neck dissection showing nodes with extranodal extension.
question: What doses and volumes do you prescribe?
answer: 66 Gy in 33 fractions to the positive margin and extranodal extension region plus 10 millimeters. 60 Gy to the postoperative bed and to the preoperative involved nodes plus 10 millimeters and involved nodal levels. 50 Gy to uninvolved dissected nodal levels and clinically at-risk nerves.
key_points: 66 Gy to margin or ENE region
Preop nodes plus 10 mm and levels
50 Gy to dissected levels and at-risk nerves
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Skin row: SCC Postop

case: A 70-year-old after wide excision of a desmoplastic melanoma of the scalp with extensive neurotropism; re-excision is not feasible for close margins.
question: Do you recommend adjuvant radiation, and what dose?
answer: Yes. Adjuvant radiation to the primary is considered for high-risk desmoplastic melanoma: head and neck location, extensive neurotropism, pure desmoplastic subtype, close margins where re-resection is not feasible, or recurrence. Dose 60 to 66 Gy in 30 to 33 fractions, or 48 Gy in 20 fractions.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Skin row: Melanoma Postop

case: A 72-year-old kidney transplant recipient with a 1.8 centimeter Merkel cell carcinoma of the arm, excised with negative margins, sentinel node negative.
question: What are the indications for radiation to the primary site and to the nodal basin?
answer: Primary site: lymphovascular invasion, immunosuppression, primary over 1 centimeter, positive or close margins, positive sentinel node, or head and neck site; so yes, about 56 Gy for an R0 bed, starting as soon as wound healing permits. Nodal basin: positive sentinel node, compromised sentinel node accuracy, or profound immunosuppression, at 50 Gy; with profound immunosuppression I would consider the basin despite a negative sentinel node.
key_points: Nodes if SLNB positive or unreliable
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Skin row: Merkel Cell Carcinoma Postop

case: An 88-year-old with Merkel cell carcinoma of the lower leg who refuses surgery, with a clinically involved inguinal node.
question: What doses and volumes do you use for definitive radiation?
answer: Definitive radiation for nonsurgical candidates, 60 to 66 Gy in 30 to 33 fractions, NCCN says 60 Gy. CTV is gross disease with a wide 5 centimeter margin; the 2 centimeter margin applies only in the head and neck. Gross nodes get GTV plus 5 millimeters to the same dose, and an unevaluated clinically node negative basin would get 45 to 50 Gy.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Skin row: Merkel Cell Carcinoma Intact

case: A 56-year-old with large pendulous breasts after right lumpectomy, planned for whole breast radiation.
question: When would you consider prone setup, and how does image guidance differ between supine and prone?
answer: Prone positioning on a prone breast board with arms up lets pendulous breast tissue fall away from the chest wall, reducing lung and heart dose and skin folds. Wire the breast borders and scar in either position. Supine uses daily kV and surface guidance such as AlignRT with weekly MV ports; prone uses daily kV or cone beam CT.
key_points: Supine: daily kV and surface guidance
Prone: daily kV or cone beam CT
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Breast row: Early Stage, Whole Breast

case: A 50-year-old after mastectomy and level I-II axillary dissection for pT3 N2 breast cancer, planned for comprehensive post-mastectomy radiation.
question: What dose options do you have, and how do you build the PTVs and their exclusions?
answer: 50 Gy in 25 fractions, or hypofractionated 42.56 Gy in 16. Chest wall CTV per RTOG atlas including the scar; PTV plus 5 millimeters excluding heart, not crossing midline, with an eval structure cropped 5 millimeters under skin. Supraclavicular PTV plus 5 millimeters excluding thyroid, trachea, esophagus, lung and vertebral body; undissected axilla plus 5 millimeters excluding lung; internal mammary plus 5 millimeters excluding heart and lung.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Breast row: Locally Advanced, PMRT

case: Post-mastectomy radiation to chest wall and supraclavicular nodes using a dual isocenter 3D technique.
question: Where are your isocenters, and how do you prevent divergence at the match line?
answer: Chest wall isocenter in the lung midway between superior and inferior borders; supraclavicular isocenter at the inferior clavicular head at the superior wire. Tangents are posterior half-beam blocked, collimator rotated to align the posterior jaw with the chest wall, and the couch rotated to avoid divergence into the supraclavicular field. The supraclavicular field is half-beam blocked inferiorly.
key_points: Chest wall isocenter midway in lung
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Breast row: Locally Advanced, PMRT

case: A 38-year-old with inflammatory breast cancer after neoadjuvant chemotherapy and modified radical mastectomy, with a residual involved unresected internal mammary node.
question: What accelerated regimen can you use, and how do you handle bolus and the unresected node?
answer: Twice-daily treatment: 51 Gy in 34 fractions BID to chest wall and nodes, then a 15 Gy in 10 fraction BID boost; daily 50 Gy in 25 then 10 Gy in 5 is the alternative. Daily 1 centimeter bolus over the chest wall. The chest wall boost covers the scar and flaps, and pre-chemo involved unresected nodes get a boost CTV of the node plus 1 to 2 centimeters, edited to anatomy.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Breast row: Inflammatory, PMRT BID

case: A 67-year-old with an ipsilateral breast recurrence 8 years after whole breast radiation, now status post repeat lumpectomy with negative margins.
question: Describe your re-irradiation volumes, technique and dose.
answer: Partial breast re-irradiation, 45 Gy in 30 fractions at 1.5 Gy twice daily with 3D conformal technique. Lumpectomy bed GTV including scar and seroma, CTV plus 1.5 centimeters cropped from outside the body and muscle, PTV plus 1 centimeter, and an eval PTV cropped 5 millimeters under skin. Daily kV or cone beam CT.
key_points: Daily kV or cone beam CT
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Breast row: Re-Irradiation, PBI BID

case: A 4-year-old has a favorable histology Wilms tumor resected by nephrectomy, with positive margins making it local stage III.
question: What is your flank radiation dose, volume, and timing?
answer: Flank RT to 10.8 Gy in 6 fractions of 1.8 Gy, starting about day 10 to 14 after surgery. CTV is the preoperative tumor plus 1 cm, including the whole adjacent vertebral body if needed to avoid a dose gradient across it, with a 5 to 10 mm PTV. Simulate supine, arms up, with a testicular shield.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Wilms Tumor postoperative, Flank

case: A 5-year-old has a stage III Wilms tumor with diffuse anaplasia after nephrectomy.
question: What flank dose do you give, and how does anaplasia change it?
answer: Anaplastic histology gets a higher flank dose: 10.8 Gy in 6 fractions plus a sequential 9 Gy in 5 fraction boost, for 19.8 Gy total. Per the sheet, that applies to diffuse anaplasia stage III at any age, and to focal anaplasia stage I to III or diffuse anaplasia stage I to II in patients 16 or older.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Wilms Tumor postoperative, Flank

case: A favorable histology Wilms tumor patient has gross residual tumor in the renal bed after nephrectomy.
question: How do you handle the gross residual disease?
