answer: Treat the flank to 10.8 Gy, then give an additional 10.8 Gy in 6 fractions boost to the residual. GTV is postoperative residual tumor on CT or MRI, CTV is GTV plus 5 mm, PTV adds 5 to 10 mm.
key_points: GTV postop residual on CT or MRI
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Wilms Tumor postoperative, Flank (gross residual)

case: A Wilms tumor patient has positive para-aortic lymph nodes at nephrectomy.
question: What is your nodal radiation field and dose?
answer: Treat the para-aortic nodes to 10.8 Gy in 6 fractions, traditionally from the diaphragmatic crus to the bottom of L5. CTV is all enlarged nodes on preoperative imaging with a 5 mm PTV. Unresected nodal disease gets a sequential 9 Gy boost to 19.8 Gy.
key_points: diaphragm crus to bottom of L5
CTV enlarged nodes on preop imaging
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Wilms Tumor postoperative, LN Irradiation

case: A 3-year-old with Wilms tumor had a preoperative tumor rupture and peritoneal implants at nephrectomy.
question: What are the indications for whole abdominal radiation and the dose?
answer: Whole abdomen RT is indicated for abdominal stage III of any histology from preoperative rupture, intraoperative diffuse spillage, or peritoneal metastases. Dose is 10.5 Gy in 7 fractions, with a sequential boost to 21 Gy for diffuse unresectable implants or gross residual disease. Children 12 months or younger are limited to 10.5 Gy total.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Wilms Tumor postoperative, Whole Abdomen

case: You are planning whole abdominal radiation for a child with Wilms tumor and peritoneal seeding.
question: How do you simulate and what are your field borders?
answer: Supine, arms up, with 4D CT to make an ITV. The CTV is the entire peritoneal cavity from the dome of the diaphragm to the pelvic diaphragm. Borders: superior 1 cm above the diaphragm dome, inferior at the bottom of the obturator foramen blocking the femoral heads, and laterally 1 cm beyond the abdominal walls.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Wilms Tumor postoperative, Whole Abdomen

case: A Wilms tumor patient has pulmonary nodules at presentation that resolve completely after 6 weeks of chemotherapy.
question: When is whole lung irradiation indicated or omitted, and what dose?
answer: Indicated for lung metastases at presentation, hilar or mediastinal node metastases, or cytology-positive pleural effusion. It can be omitted only with complete response to chemotherapy and no 1q gain or combined loss of heterozygosity of 1p and 16q. Dose is 12 Gy in 8 fractions, or 10.5 Gy in 7 fractions under age 1.
key_points: lung mets, hilar nodes, positive effusion
omit if complete response at week 6
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Wilms Tumor postoperative, Whole Lung Irradiation

case: A Wilms tumor patient with persistent lung metastases needs whole lung irradiation.
question: Describe your simulation, target volumes, and technique.
answer: Supine, arms up, 4D CT. CTV is the entire pleural surface of both lungs, ITV drawn on all respiratory phases, PTV is ITV plus 5 to 10 mm. Usually AP/PA, though IMRT or protons are options, and if the flank or abdomen will also be treated, plan the whole course upfront.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Wilms Tumor postoperative, Whole Lung Irradiation

case: You are planning flank radiation for a Wilms tumor.
question: What are your key normal tissue constraints?
answer: Remaining kidney D100 under 14.4 Gy and D50 under 19.8 Gy. Liver D100 under 23.4 and D50 under 30.6. Lungs D100 under 15 and D20 under 20. Heart D100 under 30, and spinal cord D0.03cc under 45 Gy.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Wilms Tumor postoperative, Flank

case: A child with favorable histology Wilms tumor has brain metastases and a solitary liver metastasis.
question: What radiation doses do you use for these metastatic sites?
answer: Whole brain to 21.6 Gy in 12 fractions with a 10.8 Gy local boost to fewer than 5 lesions; for more than 5 lesions, whole brain to 30.6 Gy without a boost. Liver mets get 19.8 Gy in 11 fractions, focal for one lesion and whole liver for multiple or diffuse mets.
key_points: focal for one, whole liver if diffuse
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Wilms Tumor, Brain Mets / Liver mets

case: A 3-year-old has MYCN-amplified high-risk neuroblastoma of the adrenal gland.
question: Outline the treatment paradigm and where radiation fits.
answer: Induction chemotherapy, then surgical resection, then myeloablative chemotherapy with thiotepa and cyclophosphamide and tandem autologous stem cell transplant. Consolidative radiation follows once recovered from stem cell rescue, then maintenance oral isotretinoin and the anti-GD2 antibody dinutuximab.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Neuroblastoma, High Risk

case: Same high-risk neuroblastoma patient after transplant, with residual MIBG uptake at one bone site.
question: What are your dose and target volumes?
answer: 21.6 Gy in 12 fractions. GTV is the post-induction, pre-surgery tumor respecting pushing borders, plus pre-induction involved nodes and any residual. CTV is GTV plus 1 cm cropped from uninvolved kidney, organs and bone, PTV 3 to 5 mm. Metastatic sites are treated only if still active after induction: post-induction volume plus 1 cm.
key_points: mets only if MIBG or FDG active
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Neuroblastoma, High Risk

case: You are planning radiation for a left adrenal neuroblastoma that abuts the vertebral body.
question: What are your normal tissue goals?
answer: Contralateral kidney V18 under 25 percent and mean under 14.4 Gy. Ipsilateral kidney mean under 18, V14.4 under 100 percent, V18 under 75 percent. Liver mean under 18. If the PTV enters the vertebral body, cover the whole vertebral body to at least 18 Gy to avoid asymmetric growth. Lungs V20 under 30 percent.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Neuroblastoma, High Risk

case: An infant with stage MS neuroblastoma develops massive hepatomegaly causing respiratory distress.
question: What is the role and dose of emergent radiation?
answer: Emergent low-dose radiation is used for hepatomegaly causing respiratory compromise, or orbital or optic pathway disease threatening vision. Dose is 4.5 Gy in 3 fractions of 1.5 Gy.
key_points: orbital or optic disease with vision loss
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Neuroblastoma, Emergent

case: A 7-year-old has an alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma of the forearm resected with microscopically positive margins, node negative.
question: Who needs radiation after resection of rhabdomyosarcoma and at what doses?
answer: Everyone except embryonal histology with R0 resection and negative nodes. Alveolar R0 or R1 and embryonal R1 get 36 Gy, node-positive regions get 41.4 Gy, and gross disease gets 50.4 Gy.
key_points: alveolar R0 or R1, embryonal R1
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Rhabdomyosarcoma, Postoperative RT

case: A 9-year-old has an unresected parameningeal rhabdomyosarcoma with a partial response to chemotherapy.
question: What are your dose and volumes for gross disease?
answer: 50.4 Gy, raised to 59.4 Gy for diffuse anaplasia or bulky tumors over 5 cm without complete response. GTV1 is prechemo extent, CTV1 GTV1 plus 1 cm including involved nodal basins, PTV 3 to 5 mm, to 36 Gy. Then cone down to the postchemo extent plus 1 cm, excluding areas where tumor only pushed into a cavity but keeping prechemo invasive disease.
key_points: 59.4 if anaplasia or bulky over 5 cm
prechemo GTV plus 1 cm to 36 Gy
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Rhabdomyosarcoma, Postoperative RT (gross disease)

case: A 13-year-old has a Ewing sarcoma of the pelvis after induction chemotherapy; surgery is expected to leave close margins.
question: What is the overall paradigm and the role of preoperative radiation?
answer: Induction VDC alternating with IE, then local control by surgery, radiation or both, then consolidation chemotherapy. If close or positive margins are expected, give preop RT to 36 Gy to the pre-chemotherapy GTV. Doxorubicin is held during radiation.
key_points: local control surgery, RT or both
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Ewing Sarcoma, Preop RT

case: A 15-year-old has an unresectable sacral Ewing sarcoma after induction chemotherapy.
question: What is your definitive radiation dose and volume?
answer: Definitive RT with concurrent vincristine-cyclophosphamide and IE, holding doxorubicin. 45 Gy to the pre-chemotherapy GTV volume, then cone down to the post-chemotherapy gross residual to 55.8 Gy.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Ewing Sarcoma, Definitive

case: A Ewing sarcoma of the femur is resected; pathology shows 80 percent necrosis and a margin under 1 mm.
question: What are the indications for adjuvant radiation, and the dose and timing?
answer: Adjuvant RT for close margins under 1 mm, poor histologic response with less than 90 percent necrosis, or tumor spill. Dose is 50.4 Gy to the pre-chemotherapy GTV, starting with cycle 1 of consolidation around week 14, holding doxorubicin.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Ewing Sarcoma, Adjuvant During Consolidation, Primary

case: A 12-year-old has Ewing sarcoma of a thoracic vertebral body treated with radiation for local control.
question: What are your volumes and doses?
answer: 45 Gy to the pre-chemotherapy GTV plus 1 cm, covering the entire vertebral body plus 0.5 cm, then boost the post-chemotherapy gross residual to 50.4 Gy.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Ewing Sarcoma, Vertebral Body

case: A Ewing sarcoma patient presents with bilateral pulmonary metastases and one bone metastasis.
question: What radiation do you give to the metastatic sites?
answer: Whole lung irradiation 15 Gy in 10 fractions of 1.5 Gy, with persistent nodules boosted to 45 Gy at 1.8 Gy or SBRT 30 to 40 Gy in 5. Bone mets get 45 to 56 Gy, or consider SBRT 40 Gy in 5 fractions.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Ewing Sarcoma, Lung Mets / Bone Mets

case: A 7-year-old with average-risk medulloblastoma is being simulated for craniospinal irradiation.
question: How do you simulate the patient, and when must radiation start?
answer: Supine, arms at the sides, 5-point aquaplast mask with neck rest, full-body vac-lok, and wrist straps for shoulder pulls. Radiation should start within 31 to 42 days of surgery, ideally 31 to 35. Protons preferred if available in a timely way, otherwise photons.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Medulloblastoma, Average Risk

case: You are treating craniospinal irradiation with a 3D photon technique for a medulloblastoma.
question: Describe the brain and spine fields and how you handle the junction.
answer: Brain: opposed laterals with midplane isocenter covering the cribriform plate, posterior third of the orbit and 1 cm on the temporal lobes, with collimator rotated to match spinal divergence. Spine: superior border as low as C4 to C7 without the shoulders, inferior 1 to 2 cm below the thecal sac, lateral 1 cm beyond the transverse processes with a spade covering the SI joints. Feather the junction 0.5 to 1 cm about weekly.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Medulloblastoma, Average Risk (Photon 3D)

case: A 9-year-old with medulloblastoma, who has not reached skeletal maturity, is planned for proton craniospinal irradiation.
question: How do you handle the vertebral bodies?
answer: If not skeletally mature, the whole vertebral body must be covered to at least 18 Gy to avoid asymmetric growth. Vertebral body sparing CSI is reserved for patients who have reached skeletal maturity.
key_points: vertebral body sparing only if mature
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Medulloblastoma, Average Risk

case: You are reviewing a craniospinal plan with posterior fossa boost for medulloblastoma.
question: What are your key organ at risk constraints?
answer: Brainstem surface Dmax under 58 Gy and mean under 54 with photons. Cord Dmax under 54 and D1cc under 50.4. Esophagus mean under 30, heart D50 under 15 Gy, and no more than 1 cc of brain outside the PTV receiving over 110 percent.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Medulloblastoma, Average Risk

case: A 10-year-old with group 3 medulloblastoma has more than 5 spinal drop metastases.
question: How do you modify the spinal dose and systemic therapy?
answer: With more than 5 spinal lesions, treat the whole spine to 39.6 Gy, then boost lesions to 45 to 50.4 Gy as tolerated, on top of high-risk CSI 36 Gy and posterior fossa to 54 to 55.8 Gy. Weekly vincristine is given, and adding carboplatin can be considered for high-risk group 3.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Medulloblastoma, High Risk

case: A 4-year-old has a posterior fossa ependymoma after gross total resection with no dissemination.
question: What are your doses and target volumes?
answer: Postop RT is indicated. GTV is the tumor bed, residual and resection cavity walls. CTV54 is GTV plus 5 to 10 mm, limited by bone and tentorium and no more than 3 mm into the brainstem; boost to 59.4 Gy with GTV plus 5 mm excluding brainstem, chiasm and cervical cord. PTV 3 to 5 mm. CSI only for disseminated disease.
key_points: no more than 3 mm into brainstem
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Ependymoma, Postop

case: A 12-year-old has a non-metastatic suprasellar germinoma with complete response after chemotherapy.
question: What is your radiation dose and target?
answer: After carboplatin and etoposide for 4 cycles, whole ventricular irradiation: 18 Gy for complete response or 21 to 24 Gy for partial, at 1.5 Gy per fraction. CTV is the lateral, third and fourth ventricles plus suprasellar and pineal cisterns, PTV 3 to 5 mm. Then boost the prechemo GTV plus 1 to 1.5 cm to 30 to 36 Gy for CR, or 36 to 45 Gy for PR.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Germ Cell Tumors, Pure Germinoma, Non Metastatic

case: A 14-year-old has a germinoma with positive CSF cytology and spinal leptomeningeal disease.
question: What is your radiation approach?
answer: Metastatic germinoma gets craniospinal irradiation to 21 to 24 Gy, treated first, then a boost of 9 Gy for complete response or 12 Gy for partial response after chemotherapy.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Germ Cell Tumors, Pure Germinoma, Metastatic

case: A 10-year-old has a pineal mass with elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein, consistent with a nongerminomatous germ cell tumor.
question: How does management differ from germinoma?
answer: Nongerminomatous tumors are less radiosensitive and need more chemo: carboplatin-etoposide alternating with ifosfamide-etoposide for 6 cycles. Then craniospinal irradiation to 36 Gy with an 18 Gy boost to 54 Gy total.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Non-Germ Cell Tumors, Non-Metastatic

case: A 6-year-old has a diffuse midline glioma of the pons, previously called DIPG.
question: What is your management and radiation plan?
answer: Surgery is generally not feasible and chemo has no proven benefit, so radiation alone is standard: 54 Gy in 30 fractions. GTV is tumor on T2 MRI, CTV is GTV plus 1 to 2 cm.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Brainstem Glioma, Diffuse Midline

case: An 8-year-old has a craniopharyngioma after subtotal resection with a residual cyst.
question: What is your radiation plan, and what is unique about treatment?
answer: 54 Gy in 30 fractions. GTV is residual disease and the deflated cyst on MRI, CTV plus 1 to 2 cm per the sheet, PTV 3 to 5 mm. Do weekly MRI during treatment because the cyst can grow and require replanning. For BRAF V600E mutant tumors, try vemurafenib and cobimetinib before surgery or RT.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Craniopharyngioma

case: A 15-year-old with Hodgkin lymphoma has a slow early response on interim PET.
question: What radiation doses do you use in pediatric Hodgkin?
answer: Involved-site RT 21 Gy to all initial sites of disease. Sites with slow early response get a 9 Gy boost, about 30 Gy total, and sites with partial response get a 9 to 19 Gy boost, 30 to 40 Gy total.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), Pediatrics row: Pediatric Hodgkin Lymphoma

case: A 45-year-old has a grade 2 IDH-mutant, 1p19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma after subtotal resection.
question: Is this high risk and what is the management?
answer: Yes, high risk per RTOG 9802 is age 40 or older and/or subtotal resection; RTOG 0424 used 3 or more of age 40+, tumor 6 cm or more, crossing midline, preop neurologic deficit, or astrocytoma. Management is maximal safe resection, then RT, then PCV. Alternatives include RT with temozolomide, or vorasidenib in select patients.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Glioma, Low Grade, G2 Oligodendroglioma / Astrocytoma

case: Same patient with a high-risk grade 2 oligodendroglioma.
question: What are your simulation, dose, and target volumes?
answer: Supine, arms at side, aquaplast mask, with IV contrast. 54 Gy in 30 fractions, and as low as 45 Gy may be appropriate. GTV is defined on pre and postop T2 FLAIR, CTV is GTV plus 1 to 2 cm, PTV 3 to 5 mm.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Glioma, Low Grade

case: A 38-year-old has a grade 3 IDH-mutant astrocytoma after maximal safe resection.
question: What are your dose, volumes, and adjuvant therapy?
answer: 59.4 Gy in 33 fractions with VMAT. GTV is cavity and residual covering T2 FLAIR and T1 contrast from pre and postop imaging, CTV plus 1.5 to 2 cm, PTV 3 to 5 mm. Followed by adjuvant temozolomide 150 to 200 per meter squared days 1 to 5 every 28 days for 12 cycles.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Glioma, Grade 3, G3 Astrocytoma IDHm

case: A 50-year-old has a grade 3 IDH-mutant 1p19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma after resection.
question: What is your adjuvant treatment?
answer: Radiation to 59.4 Gy in 33 fractions with CTV 1.5 to 2 cm on the cavity, FLAIR and enhancing residual, then PCV chemotherapy for 6 cycles.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Glioma, Grade 3, G3 Oligodendroglioma

case: A 55-year-old with KPS 90 has a resected IDH-wildtype glioblastoma.
question: What is your treatment regimen?
answer: Maximal safe resection, then 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concurrent temozolomide 75 per meter squared daily, then adjuvant temozolomide 150 to 200 per meter squared days 1 to 5 every 28 days, plus tumor treating fields. The same applies to grade 4 IDH-mutant astrocytoma.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Glioma, Grade 4, Good PS

case: Same glioblastoma patient, planning the 60 Gy course.
question: What are your volumes in each phase?
answer: Phase 1 to 46 Gy in 23: CTV1 is T2 FLAIR and cavity plus 2 cm, or enhancing disease plus 2.5 cm if there is no edema. Phase 2 boost 14 Gy in 7 to 60 Gy: CTV2 is enhancing disease and cavity plus 2 cm. PTV 3 to 5 mm.
key_points: T1c plus 2.5 cm if no edema
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Glioma, Grade 4, Good PS

case: A 72-year-old with glioblastoma after biopsy has KPS 60.
question: What hypofractionated options are there, and for whom?
answer: For age 60 or older with KPS over 50, 40.05 Gy in 15 fractions with consideration of concurrent temozolomide. For frail patients, age 50 or older with KPS 50 to 70, or elderly 65 or older, 25 Gy in 5 fractions. CTV is enhancing disease or cavity plus 2 cm, PTV 5 mm.
key_points: CTV T1c plus 2 cm, PTV 5 mm
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Glioma, Grade 4, Poor PS

case: A 60-year-old has recurrent glioblastoma 2 years after chemoradiation; the enhancing recurrence is 3 cm.
question: What reirradiation regimen and volume would you use?
answer: 35 Gy in 10 fractions with bevacizumab. CTV is the enhancing tumor or bed with no expansion, or up to 5 mm if under 3.5 cm or new lesions, with a 3 to 5 mm PTV.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Glioma, GBM, Re-RT

case: A 58-year-old has a grade 2 meningioma after gross total resection.
question: What are your adjuvant RT indications, dose and volume for intermediate-risk meningioma?
answer: Intermediate risk is recurrent grade 1 or grade 2 after gross total resection. Treat to 54 Gy in 30 fractions with CTV GTV plus 1 cm and PTV 3 to 5 mm.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Meningioma, Postop, Intermediate Risk

case: A 62-year-old has a grade 3 anaplastic meningioma after subtotal resection.
question: What is your radiation plan for high-risk meningioma?
answer: High risk includes grade 2 subtotal or recurrent and any grade 3. Treat 54 Gy in 30 to GTV plus 2 cm, then 60 Gy in 30 to GTV plus 1 cm, PTV 3 to 5 mm. For grade 3 with subtotal resection, consider a boost to 66 to 70 Gy at 2 Gy per fraction.
key_points: boost to 66 to 70 for G3 STR
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Meningioma, Postop, High Risk

case: A 66-year-old has an incidentally found, enlarging 2 cm presumed grade 1 meningioma near the cavernous sinus.
question: What radiosurgery and fractionated stereotactic doses would you use, and key constraints?
answer: SRS 12 to 16 Gy in 1 fraction for grade 1, 16 to 20 for grade 2. Fractionated stereotactic is 25 to 30 Gy in 5 for grade 1, 27.5 to 30 in 5 for grade 2. For single fraction, brainstem max 12 Gy and optic apparatus max 8 Gy.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Meningioma, Intact, SRS / FSRT

case: A 40-year-old with acromegaly has persistent elevated growth hormone after transsphenoidal resection and octreotide.
question: What are the radiation indications and dose options for a secreting pituitary adenoma?
answer: Indicated for failed medical management, unresectable or subtotal resection, or hormone not normalized after resection. SRS 16 to 20 Gy is preferred for faster hormone normalization; fractionated 50 to 54 Gy in 30 if over 3 cm or within 3 to 5 mm of the optic structures; or 30 to 32 Gy in 5.
key_points: failed medical therapy or persistent hormone
conventional if over 3 cm or near optics
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Pituitary Neuroendocrine Tumor, Secreting

case: A 55-year-old has a nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma with residual tumor after subtotal resection.
question: What radiation doses do you use?
answer: For subtotal resection or recurrence: SRS 12.5 to 16 Gy; if over 3 cm or within 3 to 5 mm of the optic apparatus, fractionated 45 to 50.4 Gy in 30; or 22 to 25 Gy in 5. Nonfunctioning tumors need lower doses than secreting ones.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Pituitary Neuroendocrine Tumor, Non-Secreting

case: A 52-year-old has a growing 1.8 cm vestibular schwannoma with serviceable hearing.
question: What radiation doses would you offer?
answer: SRS 12.5 Gy in 1 fraction, or fractionated stereotactic 25 Gy in 5. For large tumors over 3 to 4 cm, conventional 54 Gy in 30 fractions. No chemo role.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Vestibular Schwannoma

case: A 68-year-old with lung cancer has numerous brain metastases and will receive whole brain radiation with a 3D technique.
question: Describe your dose and field arrangement.
answer: 30 Gy in 10 fractions with opposed laterals, isocenter at midplane, collimator rotated to block the anterior orbit and tissue anterior to the skull base. Borders: 2 cm flash superiorly and posteriorly, inferior at the bottom of C1, and the anterior MLC from flash down to the front of C1, blocking lens and parotid. Daily kV imaging.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Brain Metastasis, Whole Brain, WBRT

case: A 60-year-old with 15 small brain metastases will receive hippocampal-avoidance whole brain radiation.
question: What are your volumes, constraints, and supportive medication?
answer: 30 Gy in 10 with VMAT and memantine. CTV is whole brain parenchyma to the bottom of the foramen magnum; PTV excludes a 5 mm hippocampal avoidance region with no setup margin. Hippocampi D100 under 9 Gy and max under 16 Gy; optic structures max 30 to 37.5 Gy. Daily CBCT.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Brain Metastasis, Whole Brain, HA-WBRT

case: A 58-year-old has two intact brain metastases, 1.5 cm and 2.5 cm.
question: What SRS doses and margins do you use?
answer: Lesions under 2 cm get 20 Gy in 1 fraction; over 2 cm get 27 Gy in 3 or 30 Gy in 5. GTV is enhancing tumor on T1 contrast MRI, with a 0 to 2 mm PTV.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Brain Metastasis, SRS, Intact

case: You are reviewing a single brain metastasis SRS plan prescribed to the 80 percent isodose line.
question: How do you evaluate conformity and heterogeneity?
answer: Conformity index is prescription isodose volume over target volume; 1 is perfect and higher is worse, with a goal under about 1.2 to 2. Heterogeneity index is max dose over prescription, ideally under 2; prescribing to the 80 percent line gives 1.25.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Brain Metastasis, SRS, Intact

case: A 63-year-old had a 4 cm dural-based brain metastasis resected; the cavity abuts the superior sagittal sinus.
question: What are your postoperative SRS dose and volumes?
answer: 27 Gy in 3 or 30 Gy in 5. GTV is the entire enhancing cavity and surgical tract. CTV adds 5 to 10 mm along the bone flap if there was preop dural contact and 5 mm along the venous sinus if there was preop contact. PTV 0 to 2 mm.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Brain Metastasis, Postop

case: A 62-year-old with primary CNS lymphoma is finishing methotrexate-based induction.
question: What is the role and dose of whole brain radiation?
answer: After complete response, consolidation options include WBRT 23.4 Gy in 13 fractions, cytarabine with or without etoposide, or high-dose chemo with autologous transplant. After partial response, WBRT 30 to 36 Gy with boost to residual disease to 45 Gy in 25 fractions.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Primary CNS Lymphoma, CR / PR after IC

case: A 75-year-old has medically refractory trigeminal neuralgia and is not a surgical candidate.
question: What is your radiosurgery target and dose?
answer: Target the root entry zone of the trigeminal nerve into the pons, with 70 to 90 Gy in a single fraction prescribed to the 100 percent isodose line.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Trigeminal Neuralgia

case: A 30-year-old has a 2.5 cm arteriovenous malformation in eloquent cortex.
question: What radiosurgery dose would you use?
answer: Per the sheet, radiosurgery is used for eloquent or Spetzler-Martin grade 4 to 5 AVMs. PTV equals GTV with no margin, 21 Gy in 1 fraction for lesions under 3 cm, or 18 Gy for over 3 cm.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: AVM

case: A 60-year-old has a COMS medium choroidal melanoma, 12 mm basal diameter and 5 mm thick.
question: What are your plaque brachytherapy dose and margin?
answer: I-125 plaque, 85 Gy to the tumor apex at a low dose rate around 0.6 Gy per hour. Use a 2 mm margin on the tumor border, so plaque diameter equals tumor diameter plus 4 mm, except near the optic nerve. The largest plaque is 23 mm, so about 19 mm maximum tumor diameter.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Uveal Melanoma, Brachytherapy

case: A patient with uveal melanoma is not a plaque candidate and is referred for proton therapy.
question: How is proton therapy delivered for uveal melanoma?
answer: Fiducial markers are sutured to the eye for position verification, and the dose is 50 to 70 cobalt Gray equivalent in 4 to 5 fractions.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Uveal Melanoma, Proton Therapy

case: A 45-year-old has a clival chordoma resected with positive margins.
question: What doses would you use for chordoma pre and postoperatively?
answer: Maximal safe resection then adjuvant RT, no role for chemo. Postop 70 Gy for R1 and 72 to 78 Gy for R2 gross residual, strongly considering protons or stereotactic techniques at the skull base. Preop 50.4 Gy when an R1 resection is expected. The sheet gives the same scheme for chondrosarcoma.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Chordoma / Chondrosarcoma

case: A 65-year-old with renal cell carcinoma has an isolated T10 vertebral metastasis without cord compression.
question: What are your spine radiation dose options?
answer: Intact SBRT 24 Gy in 2, 30 Gy in 3, or 30 to 40 Gy in 5 fractions. Postoperative SBRT 30 Gy in 5. Conventional palliative 8 Gy in 1, 20 Gy in 5, or 30 Gy in 10.
source: APS Boards Condensed (spreadsheet), CNS row: Spine Metastasis, SBRT Intact / Postop / Palliative

case: A 45 year old woman has a self-palpated left breast mass. Biopsy shows high grade, triple negative invasive ductal carcinoma. Ultrasound shows a 6 centimeter mass with a second biopsy-positive lesion, at least 4 axillary nodes, and infraclavicular adenopathy. CT and bone scan are negative.
question: What is the clinical stage?
answer: cT3 N3a M0, anatomic stage IIIC. Infraclavicular nodes are level III axilla, which makes it N3a.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 106-107

case: Same patient: 45 year old with cT3 N3a triple negative breast cancer, no distant disease.
question: What is your recommended systemic and surgical management?
answer: Neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy per KEYNOTE-522: pembrolizumab with carboplatin and paclitaxel, then pembrolizumab with doxorubicin and cyclophosphamide. Clip the biopsied node and mark the tumor before chemo. Then mastectomy with level I-II axillary dissection, adjuvant pembrolizumab, and post-mastectomy radiation.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 112, 118

case: Triple negative breast cancer treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, with residual invasive disease at surgery.
question: What adjuvant systemic therapy do you add, and how do you sequence it with radiation?
answer: Capecitabine per CREATE-X, which showed an overall survival benefit in patients without pathologic complete response. It is given after radiation, not concurrently. Continue pembrolizumab for a year if given preoperatively, and add olaparib for germline BRCA carriers.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 112, 115; Scripts for oral boards, Breast

case: A 45 year old had cT3 N3a triple negative breast cancer, received neoadjuvant chemotherapy, then mastectomy and axillary dissection showing a pathologic complete response, ypT0 N0, zero of 15 nodes.
question: Does she need post-mastectomy radiation, and if so to what targets and dose?
answer: Yes; base the decision on clinical stage, so clinically node positive patients get radiation regardless of response. Treat chest wall and undissected regional nodes, supraclavicular, internal mammary and level III, to 50 Gy in 25 fractions, and boost the initially involved undissected level III to 10 Gy in 5 fractions.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 122, 127

case: A woman with clinically node positive breast cancer converts to clinically node negative after neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
question: How do you manage the axilla?
answer: Sentinel node biopsy is acceptable, but to keep the false negative rate under 10 percent you need dual tracer, removal of 3 or more nodes, and removal of the clipped biopsy-positive node. If sentinel nodes are positive or she remains clinically node positive, do a level I-II axillary dissection.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 120, 123

case: A 62 year old woman had a lumpectomy for a 0.5 centimeter, ER and PR positive, HER2 negative invasive ductal carcinoma. Sentinel node biopsy shows 1 of 2 nodes positive. No lymphovascular invasion. No neoadjuvant chemo.
question: Does she need an axillary dissection, and what radiation do you recommend?
answer: No dissection; she meets Z0011 criteria: T1-2, 1-2 positive sentinel nodes, breast conservation with planned whole breast radiation, and no preoperative chemo. For this low risk patient I would give whole breast radiation with high tangents, superior border to the bottom of the humeral head.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 94-95

case: A 62 year old woman had a lumpectomy for a T1a ER positive HER2 negative ductal carcinoma. Sentinel node biopsy shows 4 of 4 nodes positive.
question: What is your recommendation?
answer: She does not meet Z0011 because she has more than 2 positive sentinel nodes, so she needs a level I-II axillary dissection, followed by whole breast radiation plus regional nodal irradiation.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 98-99

case: A 45 year old woman had lumpectomy and axillary dissection for a 6 centimeter, medial, ER positive ductal carcinoma, with zero of 10 nodes and extensive lymphovascular invasion.
question: What radiation do you recommend and what data support it?
answer: Whole breast radiation with standard tangents, with regional nodal irradiation reasonable. MA.20 included high risk node negative patients, T3 or T2 with fewer than 10 nodes removed and ER negative, grade 3 or LVSI, and EORTC 22922 included central or medial tumors; both showed improved disease-free survival but no overall survival difference.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 93, 100-101

case: A 33 year old has a self-palpated 2.7 centimeter right breast mass, ER and PR positive, HER2 1+, and a palpable mobile level I axillary node that is biopsy positive.
question: What is her clinical stage and what additional workup do you want?
answer: cT2 N1 M0, anatomic stage IIB. I would get a pregnancy test, genetics referral given age, breast MRI given young age, and consider systemic staging with CT chest abdomen pelvis and bone scan, or PET if equivocal, since she is node positive.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 134-135

case: After mastectomy and axillary dissection, pathology shows multifocal invasive lobular carcinoma, 2.2 and 0.8 centimeters, grade 2, with 5 of 22 nodes positive, no extranodal extension. ER and PR positive, HER2 negative.
question: What is the pathologic stage?
answer: pT2(m) N2a M0, anatomic stage IIIA. Four to 9 positive nodes is N2a; the pathologic prognostic stage with receptor status is IB.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 139-140

case: A premenopausal woman with ER positive HER2 negative breast cancer, pT2 N2a after mastectomy and axillary dissection.
question: What adjuvant treatment do you recommend, and what chemotherapy regimen?
answer: Chemotherapy, then post-mastectomy radiation, then endocrine therapy. Dose-dense AC then paclitaxel: doxorubicin 60 and cyclophosphamide 600 milligrams per meter squared every 2 weeks for 4 cycles, then paclitaxel 175 every 2 weeks for 4 cycles.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 142

case: A woman with HER2 positive breast cancer completed neoadjuvant docetaxel, carboplatin, trastuzumab and pertuzumab, and has residual invasive disease at surgery.
question: What adjuvant HER2 therapy do you give, and what if she had a complete response?
answer: With residual disease, switch to ado-trastuzumab emtansine, T-DM1, for 14 cycles; newer data favor trastuzumab deruxtecan. With pathologic complete response, complete one year of trastuzumab with or without pertuzumab. Add endocrine therapy if hormone receptor positive. These can be given concurrently with radiation.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 113, 115, 117; Scripts for oral boards, Breast

case: A postmenopausal woman has a pT1c N0 ER positive HER2 negative breast cancer after lumpectomy.
question: Do you order an Oncotype recurrence score, and how do you interpret it?
answer: Yes; Oncotype is indicated for ER or PR positive, HER2 negative tumors over 0.5 centimeters that are node negative, micrometastatic, or with 1 to 3 positive nodes. A score of 26 or higher recommends chemotherapy; under 26 no chemo. In premenopausal women, 16 to 25 is a gray zone where chemo benefit is not ruled out.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 33

case: A 55 year old woman had a lumpectomy with negative margins for an early stage, node negative breast cancer.
question: What whole breast dose and fractionation do you use, and what boost options?
answer: Hypofractionated whole breast, 40 Gy in 15 fractions or 42.5 Gy in 16 fractions per ASTRO. If boosting, 10 Gy in 5 fractions for negative margins, or 16 Gy in 8 fractions for a positive margin.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 35

question: According to ASTRO guidelines, which invasive breast cancer patients should get a tumor bed boost, and in whom should it be omitted?
answer: Boost for age 50 or younger, or age 51 to 70 with high grade or a positive margin. Omit if all of: age over 70, hormone receptor positive, low or intermediate grade, and margins 2 millimeters or more. EORTC boost trial lowered local failure from about 10 to 6 percent, greatest in young women, with no survival difference.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 36

case: Lumpectomy for invasive breast cancer, planning whole breast radiation.
question: Describe your breast CTV and PTV, and your boost volumes.
answer: Breast CTV is the breast tissue from the second rib insertion to the inframammary fold, sternal-rib junction to mid-axillary line, posterior border the anterior pectoralis, cropped 5 millimeters from skin. PTV is CTV plus 7 millimeters, with PTV eval cropped from skin and ribs. Boost CTV is the seroma and clips plus 1 centimeter, PTV plus 7 millimeters.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 41

case: A left sided breast cancer after lumpectomy.
question: Describe your simulation.
answer: Simulate 3 to 5 weeks after surgery or chemo, supine on a breast board with the ipsilateral arm abducted overhead and head turned away. Wire the scar and breast borders: clavicular head superiorly, 2 centimeters below the inframammary fold, mid-axillary line, and sternal-rib junction. Noncontrast CT from mandible through lungs at 3 millimeter slices, with deep inspiration breath hold to spare the heart.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 38-39, 50; Scripts for oral boards, Breast

case: Hypofractionated whole breast radiation, 40 Gy in 15 fractions, tangents only, left side.
question: What are your lung and heart constraints?
answer: Ipsilateral lung V16 under 15 percent, 20 acceptable. Contralateral lung V4 under 10 percent. Mean heart under 3.2 Gy, 4 acceptable, and for a left breast heart V16 under 5 percent. Contralateral breast max 3 Gy. These are about 80 percent of the conventional constraints.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 53

case: Conventionally fractionated post-mastectomy radiation including regional nodes.
question: What are your lung and heart constraints?
answer: Ipsilateral lung V20 under 35 percent, 40 acceptable. Contralateral lung V5 under 15 percent. Mean heart under 4 Gy, ideally lower, and heart V25 under 10 percent for left sided, under 2 percent for right sided. Contralateral breast V3 under 10 percent.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 53, 174

case: A woman is about to start whole breast radiation after lumpectomy and sentinel node biopsy.
question: How do you counsel her about the risks of radiation?
answer: Acute dermatitis and fatigue. Pneumonitis about 0.2 percent with tangents, 1 percent with nodal radiation. Late grade 2 fibrosis about 10 percent, cardiac risk about 7 percent relative increase per Gy of mean heart dose from Darby, lymphedema 2 to 3 percent after sentinel node biopsy, rib fracture about 2 percent, brachial plexopathy about 1 percent, and a small second cancer risk.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 63, 172

case: A woman had a lumpectomy for 1.5 centimeter, screen-detected, grade 2 ductal carcinoma in situ with 4 millimeter margins and a negative post-excision mammogram.
question: Can radiation be omitted, and what is the recurrence risk?
answer: Yes, omission is reasonable per RTOG 9804 criteria: 2.5 centimeters or less, low or intermediate grade, margins over 3 millimeters. Risk without radiation is about 1 percent per year, 12 year local recurrence about 12 percent versus 3 percent with radiation, with no survival difference. Offer endocrine therapy if ER positive.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 80-82

case: A 72 year old woman had a lumpectomy with negative margins for a 1.2 centimeter, ER positive, clinically node negative invasive ductal carcinoma. She will take endocrine therapy.
question: Is radiation needed?
answer: Omission is a reasonable option per NCCN category 1 based on CALGB 9343: age 70 or older, ER positive, cN0, pT1, on endocrine therapy. Ten year local recurrence is about 10 percent without versus 2 percent with radiation, with no difference in survival or mastectomy rates. She must commit to 5 years of endocrine therapy; hypofractionation or partial breast are alternatives.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 76

case: A 66 year old with a 1.4 centimeter, grade 1, ER positive, node negative ductal carcinoma after lumpectomy with negative margins wants the shortest course.
question: What partial breast technique and dose would you use, and describe your volumes?
answer: She is a good partial breast candidate. 30 Gy in 5 fractions every other day with IMRT per Florence. CTV is the lumpectomy cavity clips plus 1 centimeter, limited 3 millimeters from skin; PTV is a further 1 centimeter, limited 3 millimeters from skin and 4 millimeters into lung.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 65-67; Scripts for oral boards, Breast

case: A woman has 3 weeks of diffuse erythema and edema over half of the left breast. Punch biopsy shows invasive ductal carcinoma.
question: What is the diagnosis and T stage, and what are the diagnostic criteria?
answer: Inflammatory breast cancer, cT4d. It is a clinical diagnosis: invasive breast cancer, erythema or edema involving at least one third of the breast, and rapid onset within 6 months. Dermal lymphatic emboli alone without the clinical findings do not qualify.
key_points: at least one third of breast
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 176

case: A woman with HER2 negative inflammatory breast cancer and no distant metastases.
question: What is your overall management?
answer: Preoperative anthracycline and taxane chemotherapy, adding HER2 therapy if positive. If she responds, modified radical mastectomy: total mastectomy with level I-II axillary dissection, then comprehensive chest wall and nodal radiation. No skin-sparing mastectomy, no breast conservation, no sentinel node biopsy, and no immediate reconstruction.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 180

case: Inflammatory breast cancer after neoadjuvant chemotherapy and modified radical mastectomy.
question: What are your target, dose, and bolus?
answer: Skin, chest wall, and undissected lymphatics: supraclavicular, internal mammary and undissected axilla, to 50 Gy in 25 fractions, then a chest wall boost of 10 Gy to 60, or 16 Gy to 66 for under 45, close or positive margins, 4 or more nodes after chemo, or poor response. Daily 1 centimeter bolus.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 182-183; Scripts for oral boards, Breast

case: A 58 year old had a mastectomy and axillary dissection for a 3.2 centimeter ductal carcinoma with skin invasion, 0 of 14 nodes, negative margins.
question: What is the pathologic stage and your radiation recommendation?
answer: pT4b N0. Post-mastectomy radiation to the chest wall and regional nodes, 50 Gy in 25 fractions with bolus, and I would add a scar boost because of skin invasion.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 188-189

case: A patient is getting post-mastectomy radiation to the chest wall and supraclavicular nodes.
question: Describe your supraclavicular field borders and how you match it to the tangents.
answer: Single isocenter at the match line at the caudal clavicular head. The supraclavicular field is half-beam blocked inferiorly, angled 10 to 15 degrees off cord, superior border at the cricoid, medial border the vertebral pedicles, laterally blocking the humeral head. The tangents are half-beam blocked superiorly with no couch kick or collimator rotation.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 157, 159

case: A woman had a lumpectomy and whole breast radiation 5 years ago and now has a 1.5 centimeter in-breast recurrence.
question: What is your treatment recommendation?
answer: First choice is mastectomy with level I-II axillary staging. If she refuses and has a negative margin lumpectomy, RTOG 1014 supports partial breast reirradiation for recurrence over 1 year after radiation and under 3 centimeters: 1.5 Gy twice daily to 45 Gy in 30 fractions with 3D conformal technique.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 185; Scripts for oral boards, Breast

case: A woman completed lumpectomy and whole breast radiation and is starting tamoxifen.
question: What is your follow up plan?
answer: History and exam every 3 to 12 months for 5 years then annually; mammogram 6 months after treatment then annually. Annual gynecologic exam on tamoxifen, bone density monitoring if on an aromatase inhibitor, lifestyle counseling, and no routine imaging for metastases unless symptomatic.
source: 2024 Breast oral boards, slide 77; Scripts for oral boards, Breast

case: A man with localized prostate cancer is being considered for brachytherapy.
question: What features affect brachytherapy candidacy?
answer: Prostate size under about 60 milliliters, otherwise downsize with hormones or check for pubic arch interference; stage below T3, though T3a or b can be considered; significant outflow obstruction is a concern; and extensive calcifications favor HDR over LDR.
source: Scripts for oral boards, Prostate

case: A man with prostate cancer asks about stereotactic body radiation.
question: What features make him a poor candidate for SBRT?
answer: Significant baseline urinary symptoms with IPSS of 16 or more, bilateral hip prostheses, high risk features including MRI T3 disease, and prostate volume over 70 milliliters.
source: Scripts for oral boards, Prostate

question: How does the prostate radiation target change by NCCN risk group?
answer: Low risk: prostate alone. Intermediate risk: prostate plus the proximal 1 centimeter of seminal vesicles. High risk: prostate, any extraprostatic extension and involved seminal vesicle, with elective dose to the rest of the seminal vesicles, and the pelvic nodes if treating regionally.
source: Scripts for oral boards, Prostate

case: A man has a rising PSA after radical prostatectomy and is referred for salvage radiation with pelvic nodes.
question: What dose and fractionation do you use?
answer: 45 Gy in 25 fractions to the pelvis and prostate bed, then a sequential boost to the prostate bed to a total of 66.6 Gy in 37 fractions. If there is gross disease, a simultaneous boost to 72 to 74 Gy at about 2 Gy per fraction as constraints allow.
source: Scripts for oral boards, Prostate

question: What are the prostate brachytherapy prescription doses for LDR monotherapy, LDR boost, HDR monotherapy, and HDR boost?
answer: LDR monotherapy 145 Gy, with D90 at least 145 and V100 at least 90 percent. LDR boost 115 Gy after 46 Gy external beam, per ASCENDE-RT. HDR monotherapy 13.5 Gy times 2 implants one week apart. HDR boost 15 Gy in a single fraction.
source: Scripts for oral boards, Prostate

case: HDR prostate brachytherapy monotherapy plan.
question: What are your target goals and urethral and rectal constraints?
answer: PTV V100 over 95 percent, V150 under 35 percent, V200 under 12 percent. Urethra maximum under 120 percent and D10 under 115 percent. Rectal maximum 90 percent and V80 under 0.2 cc. Check catheter tip positions for QA.
source: Scripts for oral boards, Prostate

case: A man with intermediate risk prostate cancer will get a rectal spacer before radiation.
question: Describe the hydrogel spacer placement procedure.
answer: Fleet enema 2 hours before, hold anticoagulation, and levofloxacin 500 milligrams an hour before. Dorsal lithotomy, prep with chlorhexidine, transrectal ultrasound guidance, lidocaine near the apex. Optionally place fiducials. Advance the needle over the rectal hump, hydrodissect the plane between prostate and rectum with about 1 cc of saline, then inject the gel smoothly over 10 seconds.
source: Scripts for oral boards, Prostate

case: A man is starting prostate radiation with androgen deprivation therapy.
question: How do you counsel him on side effects?
answer: Acute: irritative and obstructive urinary symptoms and fatigue; from ADT, fatigue, weight gain and hot flashes. Late: urethral stricture, urinary frequency and hesitancy, loose stools, hematuria or rectal bleeding, and a small secondary cancer risk.
source: Scripts for oral boards, Prostate

case: A 68 year old smoker presents with painless gross hematuria.
question: What is your workup?
answer: History including smoking and occupational exposures and anticoagulation, and exam. Urine cytology, cystoscopy, CT urogram, and transurethral resection of the bladder tumor that includes muscle to stage depth of invasion. Urothelial carcinoma is the most common histology.
source: Scripts for oral boards, Bladder

case: A man with muscle invasive urothelial bladder cancer wants to keep his bladder.
question: What makes him a good candidate for bladder preservation?
answer: Good baseline bladder function, tumor under 5 centimeters, no hydronephrosis, and no extensive carcinoma in situ.
source: Scripts for oral boards, Bladder

case: A 4-year-old girl has had ataxia, nausea and vomiting for 1 week.
question: What is your workup, and which inherited syndromes do you ask about?
answer: History and exam, CBC and CMP, and MRI of the brain and whole spine with and without contrast, ideally before surgery. Ask about Li-Fraumeni from germline TP53, with a family history of breast cancer, sarcoma, leukemia, choroid plexus carcinoma and adrenocortical carcinoma. Ask about Gorlin syndrome from PTCH1 or SUFU, with multiple basal cell carcinomas and skeletal anomalies. Ask about Turcot or Lynch syndrome from APC or mismatch repair genes, with colon cancer and high-grade gliomas.
key_points: MRI brain and spine with and without contrast
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: The child with a fourth ventricle mass has a gross total resection.
question: When do you get the postoperative MRI brain, spine MRI and lumbar puncture, and why?
answer: MRI brain within 24 to 72 hours of surgery. MRI spine about 10 to 14 days after surgery if it was not done before surgery. Lumbar puncture for CSF cytology at least 14 days after surgery, to avoid a false positive from surgical debris.
key_points: Spine MRI 10 to 14 days if not done preop
LP at least 14 days after surgery
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)
flag: Differs slightly from an older note (peds-5), which says LP at 10 to 14 days; this review says at least 14 days.

case: Pathology from a posterior fossa tumor shows tumor cells arranged around a central area of fibrillary neuropil.
question: What is this finding, and which tumors have it?
answer: Homer-Wright rosettes: tumor cells surrounding a central neuropil of neurofibrillary processes. They are seen in medulloblastoma, PNETs, olfactory neuroblastoma and pineoblastoma. A posterior fossa tumor with Homer-Wright rosettes is nearly pathognomonic for medulloblastoma.
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: Final pathology after gross total resection of a medulloblastoma shows diffuse anaplasia. Spine MRI and CSF are negative.
question: What risk group is this, and what features define high risk?
answer: High risk, because of diffuse anaplasia. High risk features are residual disease over 1.5 square centimeters or M positive disease, diffuse anaplasia or large cell histology, SHH with MYCN amplification, TP53 mutation, abnormal GLI2 or loss of 14q, Group 3 with MYC amplification or isochromosome 17q, and Group 4 without chromosome 11 loss. Average risk is residual 1.5 square centimeters or less, M0, classic or desmoplastic nodular histology and no diffuse anaplasia.
key_points: Residual over 1.5 cm squared or M+
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: A child has medulloblastoma after resection.
question: What chemotherapy goes with radiation for average risk versus high risk disease?
answer: Average risk: weekly vincristine during radiation, then maintenance cisplatin, vincristine, and either lomustine on COG protocols or cyclophosphamide on St. Jude protocols. High risk: weekly vincristine during radiation, plus carboplatin for Group 3, then maintenance cisplatin, vincristine and cyclophosphamide.
key_points: Carboplatin with RT for high risk Group 3
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: You are about to simulate a young child for craniospinal irradiation.
question: How do you simulate the patient?
answer: Follow institutional standards. One approach is supine, head first, arms on the chest, 5-point aquaplast face mask and vac-lok. Scan from the vertex to the distal femur with slices of 3 mm or less, and coordinate with pediatric anesthesia.
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: Two days after posterior fossa surgery, a child develops worsening ataxia and cannot speak. Symptoms persist when radiation is due to start.
question: What is this, and would you delay radiation?
answer: Posterior fossa syndrome, remembered as SAME-R: swallowing difficulty, ataxia, mutism, emotional lability and respiratory failure, sometimes gaze palsy. It occurs in about 25 percent, about 2 days after surgery, and usually improves over 1 to 6 months, though dysarthria and ataxia may persist. Do not delay: start radiation by about day 30 to 35 after surgery, and up to day 42 is acceptable.
key_points: Start by day 30 to 35, up to 42
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: A 3-year-old with average risk medulloblastoma asks about reducing craniospinal dose.
question: What did COG ACNS0331 show?
answer: ACNS0331 randomized ages 3 to 7 to 18 Gy versus standard 23.4 Gy craniospinal irradiation, and all patients to an involved-field tumor bed boost versus a whole posterior fossa boost. Reduced dose CSI was worse: 5-year EFS 72 versus 83 percent and OS 78 versus 86 percent. The tumor bed boost was as good as the whole posterior fossa boost, with EFS about 82 versus 81 percent. So the standard is 23.4 Gy CSI with a tumor bed boost to 54 Gy.
key_points: Tumor bed boost equivalent to whole PF
source: DeCesaris, Pediatrics review didactic

case: A skeletally immature child needs craniospinal irradiation for medulloblastoma.
question: Is vertebral body sparing acceptable?
answer: The CSI CTV is the whole CSF space. Vertebral body sparing is allowed on the current COG trials ACNS2021 and ACNS2031. In the MSKCC and ProCure proton series of children aged 3 to 5, vertebral sparing gave less loss of vertebral height with similar spinal curvature, and much lower dose to the lungs, heart, esophagus, kidneys, bowel and ovaries. Traditionally the whole vertebral body was covered to avoid asymmetric growth, so say which approach you use and why.
key_points: CTV is the whole CSF space
source: DeCesaris, Pediatrics review didactic
flag: Differs from the APS sheet item (aps-peds-24), which says to cover the whole vertebral body if not skeletally mature.

case: A 4-year-old girl has a 5 cm nasopharyngeal mass. Biopsy is pending.
question: How do you work up this patient?
answer: History and exam, CBC, CMP with liver and renal function, and urinalysis. CT chest, CT or ultrasound of the liver, CT or MRI of the primary, and PET/CT. MRI brain and spine plus lumbar puncture because the primary is parameningeal. Echocardiogram before chemotherapy. Open biopsy is preferred; FOXO1 fusion means alveolar and no fusion means embryonal. Bone marrow biopsy if node positive, unfavorable histology, T2 or higher embryonal, or a positive chest CT. Add cystoscopy and exam under anesthesia for GU sites, and RPLND for paratesticular primaries in boys over 10.
key_points: MRI brain and spine and LP for parameningeal
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: A child has newly diagnosed rhabdomyosarcoma.
question: How do you assign pretreatment TNM stage, and what are the 5-year survivals?
answer: T1 is confined to the site of origin and T2 extends beyond it; a is 5 cm or less and b is over 5 cm. Stage 1 is a favorable site with any T or N and M0, about 90 percent. Stage 2 is an unfavorable site, 5 cm or less and N0, about 85 percent. Stage 3 is an unfavorable site over 5 cm or N1, about 70 percent. Stage 4 is M1, about 30 percent.
key_points: Stage 2: unfavorable, 5 cm or less, N0
Stage 3: unfavorable, over 5 cm or N1
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: You are staging a rhabdomyosarcoma.
question: Which sites are favorable, and which head and neck sites are parameningeal?
answer: Favorable sites, BONG: biliary, orbit, non-parameningeal head and neck, and GU other than bladder and prostate. Every other site is unfavorable. Parameningeal sites, IMMNNPP: infratemporal fossa, mastoid, middle ear, nasopharynx, nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses, pterygopalatine fossa and parapharyngeal space.
key_points: Parameningeal: nasopharynx, nasal cavity, middle ear, infratemporal
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: A 4-year-old has a 5 cm embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma of the nasopharynx, FOXO1 fusion negative, N0 M0. The tumor board deems it unresectable.
question: What is the stage, group and risk?
answer: Stage 2, because the nasopharynx is an unfavorable parameningeal site and the tumor is 5 cm or less and N0. Clinical Group III, because there is gross residual disease after biopsy only. That makes it intermediate risk. Low risk is embryonal stage 1 to 2 group I to II, or embryonal orbit group III. High risk is metastatic disease outside the embryonal under-10 exception.
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: An 11-year-old girl has left maxillary swelling. Workup shows a 6 cm alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma of the parameningeal region, biopsy only, N0 M0.
question: What is the stage, group and risk?
answer: Stage 3, because it is an unfavorable parameningeal site over 5 cm. Group III, because only a biopsy was done. Alveolar histology with no metastases is intermediate risk, treated per COG ARST1431.
source: DeCesaris, Pediatrics review didactic

case: A child has intermediate risk rhabdomyosarcoma.
question: What is the treatment sequence, and when does radiation start?
answer: Biopsy or surgery, then VAC (vincristine, actinomycin, cyclophosphamide) for 12 weeks, with delayed primary excision if feasible, then radiation to the primary at week 13, then more chemotherapy. High risk patients start radiation at week 20 or after chemotherapy, with consolidative RT to metastatic sites. Surgery aims for wide local excision with a 5 mm margin; extremity primaries get sentinel node biopsy, and paratesticular primaries in boys over 10 get orchiectomy and ipsilateral RPLND.
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: A child with parameningeal rhabdomyosarcoma has cranial nerve deficits at diagnosis, and the team asks for emergency radiation.
question: Would you give emergency radiation?
answer: Very rarely. Per ARST1431, emergent RT is only for symptomatic cord compression, vision loss or other function-threatening problems, and in most cases chemotherapy relieves symptoms as quickly as radiation. If it is truly needed, give the whole radiation course starting at week 1 to avoid a split course, and hold dactinomycin at week 4. A rushed plan is a sloppy plan.
source: DeCesaris, Pediatrics review didactic

case: A child with rhabdomyosarcoma is starting radiation at week 13.
question: How do you define your target volumes?
answer: GTV1 is all disease on CT, MRI and PET before any therapy. GTV2 is gross residual disease after chemotherapy, usually assessed at week 9. CTVs are the GTVs plus 1 cm, anatomically constrained, and include the whole involved nodal basin if nodes are treated. PTV is 3 to 5 mm. With residual disease, cone down after 36 Gy to the post-chemo extent, as done on ARST0531. Spare the chiasm, optic nerves, lacrimal gland, retina, brainstem, pituitary and hypothalamus.
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: A child has rhabdomyosarcoma.
question: What radiation dose do you give by clinical group?
answer: Embryonal group I gets no RT. Alveolar group I gets 36 Gy. Group II gets 36 Gy, or 41.4 Gy if nodes are positive. Group III gets 50.4 Gy, or 45 to 50.4 Gy for orbit. After delayed primary excision: R0 36 Gy, R1 41.4 Gy, gross residual 50.4 Gy. ARST1431 allowed 59.4 Gy for tumors over 5 cm at diagnosis without complete response at week 9, and 36 Gy with complete response, but dose escalation has not shown benefit in intermediate risk, so 50.4 Gy is the safest answer.
key_points: Group I alveolar and group II 36 Gy
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026); DeCesaris, Pediatrics review didactic

case: A child with rhabdomyosarcoma has metastases.
question: How do you treat the metastatic sites per ARST1431?
answer: SBRT for bone metastases under 5 cm or lung metastases: about 25 to 30 Gy in 5 fractions after complete response, or 30 to 35 Gy in 5 after partial response or stable disease. Other sites, including a bone lesion of 5 cm or more, get conventional fractionation: 40 Gy in 20 after complete response, or 50 Gy in 25 after partial response or stable disease. Bilateral whole lung irradiation is 15 Gy in 10 fractions.
key_points: SBRT for bone under 5 cm or lung
CR 25 to 30 Gy in 5, PR 30 to 35 in 5
Conventional 40 Gy in 20 or 50 Gy in 25
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026); DeCesaris, Pediatrics review didactic

case: A healthy 2-year-old has an enlarging right flank mass. Ultrasound and CT show a right renal mass.
question: What is your differential, which syndromes are associated, and what do you ask the surgeon?
answer: Differential: Wilms tumor, neuroblastoma, polycystic kidney and sarcoma. Associated syndromes: WAGR, Denys-Drash, Beckwith-Wiedemann and hemihypertrophy. Get urine catecholamines and chest imaging. Ask the surgeon about tumor spillage, lymph nodes, peritoneal implants and the contralateral kidney.
key_points: Ask about spillage, nodes, implants, contralateral kidney
source: DeCesaris, Pediatrics review didactic

case: A 2-year-old has a favorable histology Wilms tumor with diffuse abdominal spillage at nephrectomy.
question: What radiation do you give?
answer: Whole abdomen irradiation to 10.5 Gy at 1.5 Gy per fraction. WAI is indicated for stage III with cytology-positive ascites, preoperative rupture, diffuse surgical spillage or peritoneal seeding. Local spillage alone gets flank RT to 10.8 Gy at 1.8 Gy. If diffuse unresectable implants need 21 Gy, shield the remaining kidney to 14.4 Gy or less.
source: DeCesaris, Pediatrics review didactic

case: A child has stage IV favorable histology Wilms tumor with lung-only metastases.
question: When can you omit whole lung irradiation, and what did AREN0533 show?
answer: If the lung nodules completely resolve after 6 weeks of DD-4A chemotherapy (vincristine, dactinomycin, doxorubicin), they are rapid complete responders and can skip whole lung irradiation. Their 4-year EFS was 79.5 percent, short of the 85 percent goal, but OS was 96 percent. Slow incomplete responders got whole lung irradiation with regimen M, with 4-year EFS 88.5 percent and OS 95 percent. Whole lung dose is 12 Gy at 1.5 Gy per fraction, or 10.5 Gy under 12 months of age.
key_points: Omit WLI if complete response at week 6
source: DeCesaris, Pediatrics review didactic

case: A 14-year-old girl has 3 months of right leg pain and is found to have a localized pelvic Ewing sarcoma.
question: What is your management, and what radiation dose would you use?
answer: Induction VDC alternating with IE per AEWS1031, then local control, then consolidation chemotherapy. For a localized pelvic primary in a teenage girl, do not do a hemipelvectomy; use definitive chemoradiation after induction shrinks the tumor. Definitive RT is 45 Gy to the pre-chemotherapy volume plus a 10.8 Gy boost to the post-chemotherapy residual, for 55.8 Gy total.
source: DeCesaris, Pediatrics review didactic

case: A patient has Ewing sarcoma.
question: What are the AEWS1031 radiation doses for each setting?
answer: Definitive RT: 45 Gy plus a 10.8 Gy boost. Vertebral lesion: 45 Gy plus 5.4 Gy. Extraosseous tumor with complete response to chemo: 50.4 Gy. Preop RT: 36 Gy. Postop with microscopic residual and over 90 percent necrosis: 50.4 Gy to the boost volume only. Postop with microscopic residual and under 90 percent necrosis: 50.4 Gy to the larger volume. Postop gross residual: 45 Gy plus 10.8 Gy. After preop RT, add 14.4 Gy for microscopic residual or 19.8 Gy for gross residual.
source: DeCesaris, Pediatrics review didactic

case: A 17-year-old has 2 weeks of nausea, vomiting, diplopia and headache. Imaging shows a fourth ventricle mass. He has only a biopsy, showing ependymoma, and the surgeon says just irradiate.
question: What do you recommend?
answer: Complete staging with neuraxis MRI and CSF cytology. Push for maximal resection: extent of resection is the most important prognostic factor, so ask for second-look surgery aiming for gross total resection before radiation. On ACNS0831, subtotal resection got induction chemotherapy and second-look surgery, then conformal radiation.
key_points: Extent of resection is key prognostic factor
source: DeCesaris, Pediatrics review didactic

case: An adolescent has an infratentorial ependymoma after gross total resection.
question: What are your target volumes and dose per ACNS0831?
answer: GTV is the tumor bed and any residual. CTV is GTV plus 0.5 cm, anatomically confined, trimmed where invasion is unlikely and limited to the inner table of the skull. PTV per institution. 54 Gy in 30 fractions of 1.8 Gy, then a 5.4 Gy boost in 3 fractions to residual disease for 59.4 Gy; 54 Gy total is acceptable. Keep the 59.4 Gy region out of the cervical cord; do not accept a plan with a hot spot in the cord.
key_points: Keep the hot spot out of the cord
source: DeCesaris, Pediatrics review didactic

case: A 14-year-old has short stature and delayed puberty. A pituitary panel is abnormal and MRI shows a suprasellar mass. Surgeons at two hospitals refuse to biopsy.
question: What else do you need, and how do you treat a nongerminomatous germ cell tumor?
answer: Pan MRI of the brain and spine, serum and CSF tumor markers (AFP and beta-HCG) and CSF cytology. If either marker is elevated, it is a nongerminomatous germ cell tumor and tissue is not needed. Treat with carboplatin-etoposide alternating with ifosfamide-etoposide for 6 cycles, then CSI 36 Gy with an involved-field boost to 54 Gy. Whole ventricle and spinal canal irradiation to 30.6 Gy with a boost to 54 Gy is only on trial, ACNS2021. A pure germinoma would instead get whole ventricular RT plus a boost if M0.
key_points: Serum and CSF AFP and beta-HCG
source: DeCesaris, Pediatrics review didactic

case: A child has a localized germinoma treated on the ACNS1123 approach.
question: How does response to chemotherapy set the radiation dose?
answer: Carboplatin and etoposide for 4 cycles. Complete response with normal markers: 18 Gy whole ventricular irradiation plus a 12 Gy boost to the primary. Partial response with 1.5 cm or less residual: 24 Gy whole ventricular plus a 12 Gy boost. In Bartels 2020, 59 percent had a complete response and 3-year PFS with 18 Gy WVI was 94 percent.
source: DeCesaris, Pediatrics review didactic
flag: The APS sheet item (aps-peds-28) gives 21 to 24 Gy for partial response and a 30 to 45 Gy total; ACNS1123 used 24 plus 12.

case: A 65-year-old man has worsening headaches, confusion, trouble speaking and right arm and leg weakness.
question: How do you work him up?
answer: History and neurologic exam, CBC and CMP. CT head without contrast is often done first, but MRI brain with and without contrast is the gold standard. CT chest, abdomen and pelvis to rule out another primary. When describing the MRI, say the FLAIR signal may be edema or nonenhancing tumor.
key_points: MRI brain with and without contrast
CT chest abdomen pelvis for other primary
FLAIR may be edema or nonenhancing tumor
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: Preliminary pathology after resection reads high-grade glioma.
question: What else do you ask the pathologist?
answer: IDH1 and IDH2 status: wild-type means glioblastoma and mutant means it is not. MGMT promoter methylation. 1p/19q codeletion, which means oligodendroglioma. ATRX loss, which suggests an astrocytic tumor. Features of molecular glioblastoma: TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification, gain of chromosome 7 with loss of 10, and CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion. Molecular features now outweigh histologic grade, which is based on mitoses, endothelial proliferation, atypia and necrosis.
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: Pathology shows a WHO grade 4, IDH-mutant diffuse glioma.
question: What is the final diagnosis?
answer: Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, CNS WHO grade 4. Under WHO 2021, glioblastoma is by definition IDH wild-type, so an IDH-mutant grade 4 tumor is not called glioblastoma.
key_points: Not glioblastoma; GBM is IDH wild-type
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)
flag: Diagnosis wording follows WHO CNS 2021; the source slide was an image, so this answer is standard WHO 2021 naming.

case: A 65-year-old with glioblastoma, KPS 90, has had a gross total resection.
question: What is your treatment, including temozolomide dosing?
answer: Consider a clinical trial. Otherwise the Stupp regimen: 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concurrent temozolomide 75 milligrams per meter squared daily, including weekends. Then adjuvant temozolomide 150 to 200 milligrams per meter squared on days 1 to 5 of each 28-day cycle for 6 to 12 cycles, with tumor treating fields. Median survival is still about 20 months. With KPS under 60, use 40 Gy in 15, 34 Gy in 10 or 25 Gy in 5.
key_points: Concurrent TMZ 75 mg/m2 daily including weekends
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: You are contouring a resected glioblastoma.
question: How do RTOG and EORTC volumes differ?
answer: RTOG: GTV1 is the T1 contrast cavity plus residual and GTV2 adds the T2 FLAIR abnormality. CTV2 is GTV2 plus 2 cm treated to 46 Gy, then CTV1 is GTV1 plus 2 cm boosted 14 Gy to 60 Gy. EORTC: a single GTV of the enhancing cavity plus residual, CTV plus 2 to 3 cm, treated to 60 Gy with no FLAIR phase. PTV is 3 to 5 mm for both. Smaller 1 to 2 cm margins are supported, but 2 cm is the safe boards answer.
key_points: RTOG two phases, FLAIR to 46 Gy
EORTC single volume, enhancing plus 2 to 3 cm
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: You are planning a brain tumor with conventional or 2.5 Gy per fraction radiation.
question: What are your key organ at risk constraints?
answer: Conventional: optic apparatus D0.03cc under 54 Gy, brainstem under 54 to 55 Gy, spinal cord under 45 Gy, cochlea mean under 30 to 45 Gy, lens under 6 to 8 Gy and pituitary under 50 Gy. Hypofractionated at 2.5 Gy: optic apparatus under 42 Gy with V45 under 0.5 cc, brainstem under 44 Gy, cord under 42 Gy with V40 under 5 cc, cochlea under 33 Gy, lens under 9 Gy and pituitary mean under 25 Gy.
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: A patient is starting brain radiation on dexamethasone.
question: What acute radiation side effects and steroid toxicities do you counsel about?
answer: Radiation: fatigue, headache, hair loss, dry eyes, hearing changes, nausea and vomiting, seizures, and worsening of existing deficits from edema. Steroids, acute: increased appetite and weight gain, poor wound healing, gastritis so give GI prophylaxis, insomnia, irritability or mania, and immunosuppression with thrush and PJP, so give Bactrim if steroids will last over a month. Steroids, long term: cushingoid appearance, proximal muscle weakness, osteonecrosis, leg swelling, DVT and adrenal insufficiency.
key_points: PJP prophylaxis with Bactrim if over a month
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: A 39-year-old has new focal seizures and a mostly nonenhancing left frontal mass. Biopsy shows an IDH-mutant, 1p/19q codeleted oligodendroglioma, grade 2.
question: What treatment do you recommend, and what did RTOG 9802 show?
answer: She is high risk by RTOG 9802 because she had only a biopsy; high risk was age 40 or older, or under 40 with subtotal resection or biopsy. Recommend maximal safe resection if feasible, then 54 Gy in 30 fractions to the T2 abnormality followed by 6 cycles of PCV (procarbazine, lomustine, vincristine). RTOG 9802 showed that adding PCV improved 10-year PFS from 21 to 51 percent and 10-year OS from 40 to 60 percent.
key_points: High risk: biopsy or STR, or age 40 or older
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: The same 39-year-old feels well and does not want radiation or chemotherapy because of cognitive risk.
question: What could you offer, and what did INDIGO show?
answer: Vorasidenib, an IDH1/2 inhibitor, per INDIGO. INDIGO enrolled patients 12 or older with KPS 80 or more and residual or recurrent grade 2 IDH-mutant oligodendroglioma or astrocytoma after surgery within 5 years and no other treatment. Median PFS was 27.7 months versus 11.1 months with placebo, and time to next intervention improved with a hazard ratio of 0.26.
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: A young adult will receive 54 Gy for a low-grade glioma.
question: What long-term toxicities do you counsel about?
answer: Chronic fatigue, permanent hair loss in high-dose areas, endocrine and pituitary dysfunction, and neurocognitive decline.
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: A 67-year-old man has visual changes and a suprasellar cystic lesion.
question: What is your differential, what visual deficit do you expect, and what workup do you make sure was done?
answer: Supratentorial differential, COP GEMM: craniopharyngioma, optic glioma, pituitary adenoma, germ cell tumor, ependymoma, meningioma and metastasis. Chiasm compression typically causes a bitemporal hemianopsia. Workup: history, neurologic exam, CBC, CMP, a full pituitary panel, tumor markers to rule out germ cell tumor, audiometry, and an ophthalmology exam with visual fields.
key_points: Craniopharyngioma, pituitary adenoma, germ cell, meningioma
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)
flag: The visual deficit slide was an image; bitemporal hemianopsia is the standard answer for chiasm compression.

case: A patient has a sellar mass.
question: Which hormones come from the anterior and posterior pituitary?
answer: Posterior pituitary: ADH and oxytocin. Anterior pituitary: growth hormone, TSH, LH and FSH, ACTH and prolactin.
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: After subtotal resection of a suprasellar cyst, the op note describes crankcase oil fluid. Pathology is adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma.
question: What do you know about this tumor, and what is your adjuvant recommendation?
answer: Craniopharyngioma arises from Rathke's pouch, abuts the hypothalamus and third ventricle, and has a bimodal age peak at 5 to 14 and 50 to 75. Adamantinomatous is about 90 percent and has WNT pathway mutations; papillary is under 10 percent in children and about 30 percent in adults and carries BRAF V600E. Gross total resection is observed, with DFS around 70 to 85 percent but risk of vision loss and hypothalamic injury. Subtotal resection, as here, gets postoperative radiation. BRAF-mutant papillary tumors can get vemurafenib and cobimetinib. Recurrence: radiation or SRS if not previously irradiated, or intracystic bleomycin or radioactive colloid if the cyst is over half the tumor.
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: You are planning postoperative radiation for a subtotally resected craniopharyngioma.
question: What are your target volumes, and what do you watch for during treatment?
answer: GTV is residual disease including the cyst wall on MRI and CT. CTV is GTV plus 0.5 cm if you can get MRIs every 1 to 2 weeks during treatment, or plus 1 cm if not. PTV is 3 to 5 mm. The dose is usually 54 Gy in 30 fractions. About 10 to 12 percent of cysts grow during treatment and 20 to 30 percent within 6 months after, which may need drainage or replanning.
key_points: CTV 0.5 cm with frequent MRI, 1 cm without
Cyst growth may need drainage or replanning
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)
flag: The APS sheet item (aps-peds-32) gives a 1 to 2 cm CTV; this review uses 0.5 to 1 cm based on imaging frequency.

case: Two weeks into radiation for craniopharyngioma, a patient becomes acutely confused. Labs show high serum sodium.
question: What is happening, and how do you treat it?
answer: Central diabetes insipidus. It occurs in about 60 to 70 percent after surgery, and about 30 percent can still develop it after radiation. It causes polyuria, thirst and hypernatremia. Treat with free water replacement, which is favored initially after surgery, and desmopressin, and check urine and serum osmolality frequently.
source: CNS/Peds mock oral boards review (March 2026)

case: A 42-year-old woman presents with postcoital bleeding and a visible cervical mass. Biopsy shows squamous cell carcinoma.
question: What is your workup?
answer: Full history and pelvic exam including speculum, bimanual and rectovaginal exam to assess size, vagina, parametria and sidewall, plus nodal exam. Labs including CBC, CMP for renal function, pregnancy test and consider HIV. Pelvic MRI and PET/CT for stage IB1 and above, with cystoscopy or proctoscopy if concern for bladder or rectal invasion.
source: 2024 Gyn oral board - EM final, slide 14

case: A woman has a 4.5 centimeter squamous cell carcinoma confined to the cervix. MRI shows no parametrial or vaginal extension and PET shows no nodal disease.
question: What is the FIGO stage?
answer: FIGO 2018 stage IB3: invasive carcinoma confined to the cervix, greater than 4 centimeters.
key_points: Confined to cervix, greater than 4 cm
source: 2024 Gyn oral board - EM final, slide 15/43
flag: AJCC 9th cervix uses FIGO 2018, so the stage is unchanged.

case: A woman with cervical squamous cell carcinoma has tumor extending into the lower third of the vagina, without pelvic sidewall extension or hydronephrosis. Nodes are negative.
question: What is the FIGO stage?
answer: FIGO stage IIIA: involvement of the lower third of the vagina. Upper vaginal involvement would be IIA.
source: 2024 Gyn oral board - EM final, slide 43
flag: AJCC 9th cervix uses FIGO 2018, so the stage is unchanged.

case: A woman has a 5 centimeter cervical squamous cell carcinoma with parametrial involvement not reaching the sidewall. PET shows an FDG-avid left external iliac node, and the para-aortic nodes are negative.
question: What is the FIGO stage?
